May 2, 1988
Canadian Environmental Protection Act

The House resumed from Tuesday, April 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. McMillan that Bill C-74, an Act respecting the protection of the environment and of human life and health, be read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: When Bill C-74 was last before the House, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) had completed her speech. The question and comment period following the Hon. Member's speech is now available to Hon. Members.

Mr. Speaker, the other day I listened to my hon. colleague's speech on this legislation. I want to ask the Hon. Member how she feels about the approach taken in this Bill and whether the approach the Government is suggesting is the appropriate one. She is knowledgeable in this area, and I think it is important that we are aware of just how the Government approaches an issue or challenge in a particular piece of legislation. Perhaps she would want to comment on that.

Mr. Speaker, I want to point out a number of ways in which the approach to the Bill is seriously flawed. We went into great detail with some amendments and in some respects a better Bill came back, but the Government has been doing the wrong thing.
I would like to quote some remarks made by Professor Ross Hume Hall who in fact will be involved in the administration of this Bill. He says very strongly that the whole approach taken by the Liberals in the past under the old Environmental Contaminants Act and this Bill does not do the job that needs to be done. He said:
The 1987 act should be scrapped in favour of a radically different approach to the control of chemical pollution, an approach which can be stated in two words: don't pollute. Ask the question, "how do chemicals get into the environment?," and then set up legal procedures to block the sources of pollution. No one action prevents pollution. It requires actions on sewage, waste dumps, disposal of household garbage, improved incineration, recycling, and prohibition of products that can't be disposed of without contamination.
Such a comprehensive approach takes time and effort to work out. But in the end, we will have an industrial society in which chemicals continue to play an important role, but which will be used and disposed of without polluting the environment.
To do that, we would have to go back to square one. I do not want to be too critical of the Conservative Government because the faults in this Bill were in the old Liberal legislation. This legislation deals with environmental contaminants and chemical pollutants one at a time, without looking at them in interaction and without looking at their cumulative effects. It goes on the basis of lab tests and hopes for the best. That is a very cumbersome procedure. We know that it took five chemicals 10 years to get on the list under the old process and
that the new process will not speed things up. The desire to do something about this is not there.
Professor Hall tells us not simply to blame the weak Department of the Environment, although he blames the weak Department of the Environment in many respects. He said:
A parade of 11 ministers of environment, either disinterested or politically feeble, has passed through the department since 1972. Successive federal governments (Liberal and Conservative) have encouraged weak management, preferring the Department of the Environment to be like a declawed and neutered tomcat, showy, but unaggressive and docile.
We still see the same thing in this Bill. Let me give an example of the approach used by the Bill and what is wrong with that approach.
The toxicology that Health and Welfare uses to test food additives and drugs is laboratory toxicology. It consists of relatively short-term tests on animals and it fails to predict toxic effects, particularly effects in humans. Professor Hall refers to a National Research Council of Canada report on the toxicity of dioxins, a serious environmental contaminant. This provides an illustration of the impossibility of predicting human effects.
A scientist working with dioxins accumulated traces of the substance over a period of time. He began to experience nightmares at night and an inability to concentrate during the day. He suffered from headaches, memory loss, and impotence. The constellation of toxic effects devastated this man. This happened to a human being. The tests, however, are done on rats and guinea-pigs. Have you ever asked a rat if he has a headache, Mr. Speaker? Obviously we do not know what happens to these lab animals.
No laboratory experiments on animals can predict the toxic effects on humans of long-term exposure, to small amounts of chemicals. We only happen to know of these effects of dioxin in humans because of accidental exposure which is neither systematic nor a desirable method of gaining toxicological information.
I welcome the opportunity to expand a bit on what is wrong with the approach, which is that the Bill goes after things one at a time and will not make a significant impact in reducing contaminants in the environment.
The process is cumbersome and we really ought to be doing what Professor Hall suggests we should be doing, which is reducing substantially contaminants entering the environment and having a whole strategy to do that, including a strategy for how we dispose of our garbage and consumer products. We must begin to do that if we really want to be serious about cleaning up the environment.

Mr. Speaker, the Member made some reference to criticism of the previous Liberal legislation with regard to the environment. The Liberals criticized this legislation, saying that it was inadequate and that they would have done better. Since they quoted the same expert in their
May 2, 1988

presentation, could the Member explain to us what this expert said with regard to previous Liberal efforts in the matter of environmental legislation?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to answer that. This world renowned expert said that the past performance of the Liberal Government was not very good either, that we have the same flaws in this very cumbersome approach as we had in the old Bill. His blame was directed to the present Government.
He used the analogy of a bridge that falls down. Would anyone hire the same architect and the same engineers and tell them to come up with the same design to rebuild the bridge? Clearly we would not do that. Anyone would be irresponsible to do that. The model in the previous legislation is simply not adequate but the model was followed again in this legislation.
Therefore, there has been a failure to learn on the part of the present Government. Let us not go back to a rosy past when the enforcement procedures were very much better, because that is simply not true. We have a very weak and cumbersome approach which accepts that we will have an enormous amount of pollution. However, we are going to name only some criminals and there will be some contaminants that we will not allow. A special process will be set up to identify them and they will be put on a list. This process will take a very long time as it did when it was set up by the previous Government.
Professor Hall gives an interesting example of PCBs. The toxicity of the substance was well established in 1976 and manufacturing of the substance actually stopped. One would have thought it would be simple to write a regulation under the old legislation given that that was the case. However, it was not simple. The process was cumbersome. The President of the Iron Ore Company of Canada was one Brian Mulroney, and the Iron Ore Company of Canada and other industries raised objections to a regulation of PCBs. It is scandalous to think that objections were raised by none other than the present Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) to getting rid of one of the most dangerous contaminants known, the toxicity of which had been well established.
As a New Democratic critic of the environment I want to be very clear that the deficiencies belong to both Governments; they belong to the process. If we really want a safe environment and really want to change our ways, we will have to develop a strategy which will include many elements right from packaging to consumer practices, municipal incineration, and recycling. It is time that we got down to developing real strategies which will actually improve the environment rather than only picking away, item by item, substance by substance, review committee by review committee, to provide this very modest amount of protection against only the most serious contaminants.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary. We all appreciate that supposedly the most efficient way to do business is as it is found in totalitarian regimes, where Governments do not have to worry about Parliaments and do not have to be concerned about open and thoughtful debates.
It is a little odd that within the first few hours of this week the Government has sent the signal to the Opposition that it plans to use whatever measures are at its disposal to curtail debate and muzzle the House of Commons. It will limit the ability of the Opposition or government Members to participate in debate.
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
I take this as the Government serving notice that it plans to use its majority in the House of Commons to curtail discussion of the environment.
The days when we have talked about the environment, whether about global environment conditions or local crises, have been very few and far between. As a matter of fact, I cannot recall any days, with the exception of the Opposition Parties using their opposition days to carry on that kind of debate. I find it inappropriate that the Government would now limit debate, that it would muzzle parliamentarians by moving, in a sense, a form of closure. If the Government is hoping to get co-operation to make the House of Commons work effectively and efficiently, this is not the way to do it.
I regret that the Government once again fails to appreciate the traditions of a parliamentary democracy. But what can one expect from a political Party that saw fit to storm the Speaker's chair not many months ago and bring the House of Commons to its knees day after day after day? I remember the spectacle. I can say as a parliamentarian that it was certainly the darkest day of my life when I realized that Members of Parliament of the Progressive Conservative Party believed that Parliament ought not to continue, that it should be brought to a close. We saw the spectacle day after day of bell ringing, and we saw a political Party participate in the ultimate abuse of the parliamentary system and traditions-and some of them now are laughing. They must think that this muzzling of debate is very humorous. But it is only Monday morning, and it is only the first indication of that sad tradition being adopted by the Government's parliamentary leadership.

Mr. Speaker, as usual, I listened with great care to my friend across the way. He raised rather repeatedly a matter of great principle affecting the fundamental nature of this country, namely, a constitutional proposal back in 1980, which did indeed cause this Party, then in opposition, to use all the procedural aspects available to us to filibuster and cause change. It was a matter of fundamental principle.
I think a careful reading of our precedents and the patterns of this House would indicate that the rules exist with some looseness so that, on matters of great principle, a minority of the House can use the rules to bring these matters to the attention of Canadians and to cause perhaps change to take place. That is our tradition, and that is why it was done.
I suggest that the Member may be speaking from the heart, but he should perhaps reconsider in his head what constitutes abuse. Working within the rules and using the rules to advantage on matters of great principle, I suggest is not abuse. However, to use those same rules and those same opportunities to filibuster legislation, related, for example, to relief for victims of crime to set up an opportunities agency in Atlantic Canada, to help Atlantic Canadians to get jobs, to do the same in western Canada to help western Canadians get jobs, and to

May 2, 1988
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
clean up the environment, that is where the true abuse lies. That is abuse of the rules of this Chamber.
The Hon. Member raises the issue of closure. The calendar provides for closure on Monday at one o'clock with a recommencement at two o'clock. The calendar on Monday provides for closure at five o'clock. There is an automatic closure. By eating up the time of this House in questions and comments and repetitive speeches which stop us from getting to important matters the Opposition, and in particular the New Democratic Party on most occasions is using two closures a day. How long can they continue introducing motions for six-month hoists and recycling their speakers on the same issue? Because of the nature of the parliamentary calendar there is closure twice a day, and I suggest the Opposition since Easter-starting before, but clearly since Easter-has been using those two closure opportunities every day to grind this place to a halt so that the things Canadians need cannot come about.
On this Bill there is absolutely no abuse by the Government. No thoughtful person in this country would believe that this Bill has not had all the vetting, scrutiny, and free speech it so rightfully deserves because the environment is so important. But there comes a time, when months have passed, when witnesses have been heard, when amendments have been made, where we should bring this item to a close. We should put the law in place so that we and our children will have a better environment. It is not the time for further talk. It is the time for action.

The Government wants to get rid of questions and comments. It wants to get rid of third reading entirely. It wants people to speak in this House only if the Government says so. That is the Government's version of democracy. The Government tells us the rules are all right when, somehow or other, Members can get away with going up to the Speaker's chair, shaking their fist and threatening physical violence because they do not like the ruling of the Speaker. That is all right for the Tories. What they do not like is honest and reasonable debate. There they are in their true colours. History has proven that any time a tyrant wants to close off the democratic process, that tyrant
always says: "I am doing it for the best of motives", but that does not change anything. There is something very wrong with what the Member is saying. He is saying in effect: "Do it our way or do it not at all". That is Tory democracy.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-74 respecting the Canadian Environmental Protection Act is a measure that does take some limited, tentative but potentially useful steps in the direction of further improvement of the protection of our environment. I say this in spite of the obvious shortcomings and imperfections in the Bill. Let us recognize that in the time since the Conservative Government was elected it has taken all too many backward steps which provide reason, good reason, for very legitimate skepticism concerning its resolve in following through on whatever positive aspects Bill C-74 may have.
Since September, 1984 the Conservative Government, by way of just one example of what I am talking about, has drastically cut back funding for the Canadian Wildlife Service, which has limited the Service's capacity to conduct research into toxic chemical effects on wildlife. This is a research activity that provides important preliminary scientific clues to indicate what effect chemicals discharged into our air, water, and land have on the health of Canadians.
In November, 1984 the Conservative Government eliminated the funding previously pledged by the previous Liberal Government for the toxicology research centres proposed by the Universities of Guelph and Toronto. If these centres had gone ahead, if they were now in place, they would not only be carrying out important research but they would be providing answers to concerns we have about toxic chemicals. This cut was only one part of the $48 million in cuts in spending that the Conservative Government has made in past years from the total government budget for the environment.
The Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) silenced his Environment Canada research officers when they tried to tell the truth to Canadians about the dangerous levels of toxic chemical contamination in general and in particular about the levels of contamination in the St. Clair River. In November, 1985 the Minister of the Environment turned down a request by the Great Lakes Institute of the University of Windsor for a grant of $100,000, which would have enabled the Institute to have continued its urgently needed and outstanding work on the issue of the toxic blob in the St. Clair River. By removing this mandate the Government lessened-in fact it undermined-the Institute's capacity to provide research leadership in solving the problems of toxic chemical pollution like that of the toxic blob in the St. Clair River.
I was able to find out and tell the House and the public that it appeared that the federal Department of the Environment sat for a year on a chemical sample obtained by the Great Lakes Institute from the St. Clair River which would have brought out the problem of the St. Clair River blob about a

May 2, 1988
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
year earlier than in fact was the case. So much for commitment and concern when it comes to real action to deal with problems of the environment.
Let us remember also that the Government withheld the Storm Warnings Report on the build-up and circulation of toxic chemicals through our air, soil, and water, the very same toxins that emerge in our food supply.
Under the best of circumstances it would be hard to prevent our environmental law and the associated enforcement rules and regulations that control and reduce harmful toxic substances in our air, water, and soil, from lagging behind the increasingly rapid development in technology and the ongoing introduction of new chemical substances. But it is still to be proven whether Bill C-74 can be at all effective in regulating toxic substances and whether, as the Government originally stated, it can serve as a foundation for more comprehensive protection of our environment.
We already know that Bill C-74 itself will not contribute to enforcing the repair of previous environmental damage in the St. Clair, Detroit, St. Lawrence, and Niagara rivers, to name but a few examples.
Back in October, 1986 I called for the creation of a super fund as part of a joint federal-provincial effort to deal with the problems of the high cost of the clean-up of toxic chemicals. Even though the Government indicated some openness to this idea, nothing at all has happened. The legislation before us today does nothing to enable the creation of such a fund. Among other things, a super fund would help pay for the clean-up of chemical wastes which have been dumped in burial sites across the country.
Bill C-74 will not provide a straightforward set of rules to assist in the regulation of chemical breakdown products such as dioxins. It will not regulate pesticides, herbicides, and the food and drug additives which are currently covered under other statutes. This Bill does not even specify the chemicals to be controlled after it becomes law.
Also, Bill C-74 was supposed to be a consolidation of the many existing federal environmental laws but it only includes the Clean Air Act, the Ocean Dumping Control Act, and Part III of the Clean Water Act. In addition, there is a well recognized and widely agreed upon need for these laws to be updated and strengthened, but Bill C-74 does not deal with this need in any way, shape, or form.
Bill C-74 will have no impact on the reduction of acid rain from Canadian sources or otherwise. We saw last week how the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) continues to boast about his special relationship with President Reagan of the United States, and the value of this relationship. He signed a trade deal with the United States that will surrender vitally important elements of control by Canadians over their own social, economic, and cultural affairs. However, the most recent of his
four annual summit meetings has again failed totally to move the United States Government toward even a plan for reducing its sulphur dioxide emissions, a key cause of the very serious problem of acid rain. In fact, last week we learned that the United States is pressing agencies of the United Nations for relaxation of previously negotiated international limits on emissions that cause acid rain.
In its original form, Bill C-74 did not stop the export of toxic substances that are banned in Canada. These exports are now prohibited by the Bill, because the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), the Liberal critic for the environment, worked long and hard on behalf of the Liberal caucus to bring about amendments. However, this legislation does not follow through upon the Minister's promise of April, 1986 to establish an environmental bill of rights.
Upon his introduction of Bill C-74 on June 26 of last year, the Minister of the Environment took great pains to point out and emphasize the severity of penalties to be applied against those convicted of crimes against the environment. Executives of companies that pollute the environment will face jail sentences and fines of up to $1 million per day.
We in the Official Opposition agree strongly with the imposition of the appropriate penalties, but we are concerned that the Conservative Government will neither provide the resources required to detect violations that cause environmental damage, nor exert the leadership required to prosecute and secure imposition of the new, higher penalties.
The Government has committed the paltry sum of $37 million to be allocated among three government agencies over five years to finance the work of assessing substances already in existence, and new chemicals before they are marketed. That is not all. This same $37 million will have to finance enforcement of the legislation in the field over that same five years. Surely this is absurd.
There are approximately 60,000 chemicals already circulating in our environment, and we can expect the future introduction of 1,000 or so per year. According to the information provided by highly regarded experts in the pollution control field, the single chemical approach to compliance research carried on by the designated government agencies will take
38.000	person-years to develop regulations on just 1,000 of the
60.000	chemicals currently in existence. How can the agencies involved even begin to examine the 1,000 new chemicals brought into use each year?
These projections have been published by Dr. Ross Hume Hall of McMaster University, a former member of the Canadian Environmental Advisory Council. He bases his findings on the most recent record of the Government's own Contaminants Control Branch. This branch is staffed by only 19 people; it has produced control regulations at the rate of one chemical for every two years. In my view, Canadians have absolutely no reason to believe that the compliance and enforcement provisions contained in Bill C-74 will either reduce the rate of introduction of new pollutants or redress, in
May 2, 1988

any significant way, the damage already done. Canadians are concerned that the Government will continue its record of failure to devote the expertise and financial resources required to begin solving the real problems of pollution.
What does this mean to ordinary Canadians? For some two years I have been trying without success to get the Conservative Government to contribute funds to help the provincial and municipal Governments to upgrade outdated sewage treatment systems located in the Windsor area, and similar cases in other parts of the country. Fortunately, the Peterson Government of the Province of Ontario has stepped in to begin the work. However, the inaction of the federal Government means that this will take a lot longer, and it will likely cost the municipal taxpayers much more than if the federal Conservative Government was in fact doing its fair share.
In the City of Windsor problems have to be solved that have been caused by the inadequate facilities at the Little River sewage treatment plant. Problems have to be solved that are caused by the existence of more than 4,000 septic tanks on the west side of Windsor and Sandwich West Township which overflow and discharge into the Detroit River through Turkey Creek. There must be new joint programs created by the federal and provincial Governments to respond to these and similar infrastructure needs across the country.
I have made repeated representations to the Minister of the Environment, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) who has responsibility for Canada's involvement in international waterways.
In spite of these representations, the Government has failed to commit itself to doing what should be its full part to solve these types of problems. It refuses to accept its role in putting up the money to maintain, renew, or upgrade facilities that, in turn, provide our clean water. Its refusal contributes to a deteriorating situation that jeopardizes the health and wellbeing of Canadians. Yet, even though the Government argues that it should not do this because it is not a federal matter, there are well established precedents for the federal Government assuming its share of financial responsibility. Examples include the former federal Government's municipal loan fund as well as its urban transportation assistance program, another area which some have argued is not under federal jurisdiction when it comes to municipal roadways and provincial highways. There is a federal role in infrastructure for our cities, towns, and municipalities. It is something which involves the health and safety of Canadians and it involves the well-being of the entire economy.
In Windsor and Essex County the people are very concerned about the huge garbage incinerator being built by the City of Detroit, without the necessary pollution control equipment to prevent the discharge of dangerous toxic chemicals into our air. They ask the questions: "Is the federal Government really doing enough to help bring about the installation of this pollution control equipment? Is it making full use of the Great
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
Lakes Water Quality Agreement and the Boundary Waters Treaty, which also covers the airborne pollution of our boundary waters to help deal with this situation?"
I have urged both the Ontario provincial and the federal Government to take every action possible both under existing international agreements, like the ones I have mentioned, as well as the laws of the State of Michigan and of the United States to help bring about a meaningful solution to this problem. In my view the Conservative Government, in spite of the honeyed words of the Minister of the Environment, is not being sufficiently active to press the Canadian case in preventing the Detroit incinerator from being built and operated without the necessary air pollution control equipment. In effect, the Ontario Government has been left on its own to defend the Canadian environmental interests by taking the issue to the courts of the State of Michigan.
Through my own direct inquiries of the Office of the Governor of Michigan, I discovered that there were no less than six possible incinerator projects that might go ahead in the Michigan area near the international boundary, projects that the State of Michigan was aware of but Environment Canada and External Affairs did not seem to know anything about them. As a result I called for an early warning system to be set up to allow Canadian authorities, both federal and provincial, to be aware of such projects that could affect Canadians at a very early stage. This step would permit sufficient time for studies to be carried out and representations to be made in order to prevent these projects from going ahead, unless they had all the necessary pollution control equipment to ensure the protection of the health and safety of Canadians.
The federal Department of the Environment first stated that existing forms of consultation were sufficient. However, after I pressed the matter and pointed out the significance of this list of projects that I discovered, not too long ago the Minister of the Environment finally agreed with me to set up such a system in co-operation with the United States federal and state authorities and the Province of Ontario.
These are not the only important environmental issues concerning the people of Windsor and Essex County which require immediate and urgent action at the international level. The Fermi II nuclear generating plant owned by Detroit Edison and located in Munroe, Michigan is just a short distance from the international border and the 300,000 people living in the Windsor-Essex County area. They are not satisfied that there is absolutely no risk to their health and safety if that plant continues to be allowed to operate at full power.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has rejected my request that the Canadian Government seek the agreement of the United States Government for a reference to the International Joint Commission to permit permanent and ongoing

May 2, 1988
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
monitoring of the safety of the Fermi II nuclear power plant and similar power plants on both sides of the border. This reference would be carried out by the International Joint Commission, but agreement by both the Canadian and American Governments is required for it to be done. I have asked the Minister to review his decision, to re-open it, and to take a fresh look because the International Joint Commission has a track record of looking into these kinds of questions. However, it cannot carry out the job that it could do without agreement of the Canadian and American Governments.
In the meantime I have contacted the Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency to request that it constitute an Operational Safety Review Team to examine the Fermi II reactor in order to assure, if possible, the people of Windsor and Essex County that all the necessary safety requirements applying to Fermi II are being fully met.
What I have been talking about shows that the current Conservative Government is not doing nearly enough to preserve and protect our environment. This piece of legislation we are currently discussing, Bill C-74, is only one small and limited step-I admit a step in the right direction-which will be of value only if the Conservative Government can be relied upon to summon the will power to devote the necessary resources toward the effective enforcement of its provisions.
The Government's record on environmental matters since it took office does not give us good reason to be optimistic. The people of Canada have demonstrated that they consider protection of the environment both in Canada and around the world to be a number one priority for their Governments, federal and provincial. They want in particular this federal Government to do more than it has done already.
While Bill C-74 deserves some support, we have to recognize it for the limited step it is and to reiterate that to be meaningful there must be a greater commitment than has been shown in the past by the Conservative Government to enforce this Bill, to carry out its responsibility within Canada and in the world, and to help Canadians as members of the great family of the world to a clean and healthy environment. Without it, our world and its future are at risk. Canadians are calling for action and we in turn call upon this Government for action, action it has unfortunately not shown up to now.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) has demonstrated in his intervention today how concerned he is about the quality of the environment for citizens in Windsor and that region. He has also outlined a number of initiatives that he has taken which are very impressive, both in the field of water quality and air quality, as well as in ensuring that plans for the construction of incinerators on the other side of the border will not impair or affect the health of the population in his area.
The Member has also made a reference to an operational safety review team that he has requested from the Atomic Energy Agency, which is a very creative and imaginative idea
that would help considerably in laying the foundation for a better approach in the construction of future plans in that area.
1 would encourage the Hon. Member for Windsor West, because of the limited time he had in making his presentation, to expand on any of these initiatives so that the citizens in his area will have the full flavour and understanding of what he has attempted to do. Evidently his efforts are not being listened to carefully by federal authorities and the federal Government here in Ottawa. As he already pointed out there are gaps between the rhetoric being expounded by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) and in moving to meet the real needs in certain areas.
Would the Hon. Member for Windsor West give us a deeper insight into the situation as he assesses it in his area?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Davenport has raised some important points. I will attempt to deal with them briefly. Over all what we need to see on the part of this Conservative Government is a greater willingness as the voice of Canada in dealing with other countries, particularly the United States to speak up and be more vigorous in defence of Canadian interests.
If there is a special relationship between the Prime Minister and Ronald Reagan, then why is it not made use of in some constructive way? We have already had it demonstrated that this special relationship is worse than useless when it comes to acid rain. Why has the Prime Minister not used the special relationship to get the American Government to press the City of Detroit not to go ahead with the Detroit garbage incinerator without the necessary pollution control equipment? Why has the Prime Minister not used the special relationship to ask the American Government to take more seriously than has been the case until now the concerns of the people in the Windsor area about the Fermi II nuclear generating plant?
One thing I did not mention in my speech is that I and other Members of Parliament for the area, involving all three political Parties, made a formal appeal to the full nuclear regulatory commission of the United States when the regional office of that commission, based in Chicago, granted a few months ago authority to Detroit Edison to operate the Fermi II plant at full power in spite of the record of technical and personnel problems and the concerns expressed in the assessment reports of the nuclear regulatory commission's own staff. We made this appeal to the full commission. The commission has accepted our appeal and is studying it.
I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs to join with us in formally supporting our appeal, but we have had no agreement so far. I have asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs to support my formal request to the Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency for the setting up of a special operational safety team to review Fermi II, but I have had no response to this request so far. I would think the Secretary of State for External Affairs should
May 2, 1988

support this request, because it is to an agency of the United Nations and Canada is a member of the agency and supports its work. I look forward, hopefully in this case, to a favourable response.
What is missing here is a sense of purpose, commitment, and action to go along with the very nice language that we hear all the time from the federal Minister of the Environment. Certainly it would be hard to surpass him for rhetoric when it comes to the matter of protection of the environment. When one peels off the various covering layers on that rhetoric or if one waits awhile to see what happens after the rhetoric, one finds very little there. That is all too bad, because even though we do not support this Government, even though we think it is a bad Government that should be replaced, it is in power and it does have an opportunity to act. It is not doing its job in this matter of the environment, as it is not doing its job in so many other areas of importance to Canadians.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the House Leader for the Liberal Party has spoken at third reading and not before. If it is not the intention of the Liberal Party of Canada to contribute to the filibuster on the protection of the environment, I wonder if I could at least have a commitment from the House Leader of the Liberal Party. If speaking out on behalf of constituents is what the Liberal Party would like, would he indicate to the House that he is prepared to sit through the luncheon adjournment so that freedom of speech can prevail and so that Hon. Members do have a chance to speak on behalf of their Parties?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a new definition of filibuster here. For the Government, filibuster begins after three speeches, one of which is the Government's own speech. The Hon. Member is reflecting on the quality, value, and necessity of the Government's own spokesman on this Bill. If that is a filibuster, why did he not prevent a Conservative from speaking on third reading? I hope the record will show what the Hon. Member who is speaking on behalf of the Government thinks about the value, quality, and content of the speech made by the spokesman for the Conservative Party when third reading stage began.
The rules of this House, supported with great fanfare by the Hon. Member's Government, provide for breaks at the noon hour and in the evening. If the Hon. Member did not like that, why did he and his Party support those rules? Why have they been going around the country boasting about how these rules which include these breaks are models of parliamentary reform? The Government had the majority to prevent the stipulation of times for adjournment, but it included that stipulation because it recognized that breaks to enable people to get in touch with their offices, and, yes, to have lunch or supper from time to time, contribute to a better quality of consideration of issues in the House of Commons.
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
The Government controls what measures are brought before the House when it pertains to government business. If the Government has something more important than this Bill that it wants to deal with, it can substitute without any notice whatsoever any other measure it wants and which it considers more important.
I hope the Hon. Member does not think that he is fooling anyone with the suggestion that some reasonable debate on third reading, which is provided for in the rules and has been part of British and Canadian parliamentary procedure for hundreds of years and which has remained in the rules after parliamentary reform, is in any way an abuse or a filibuster.
Instead, if the Hon. Member thinks there is something more important than this Bill-and that is what he seems to be saying because the point of what he said was that the speech given by the Conservative Member in support of the Bill was useless-and if he says that further debate on this Bill should not go on, I challenge him to call another measure that he considers to be more important. If he does not do that, he will be exposed as the sham that he, his Party, and his Government really are.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be able to speak about some of the same concerns about which the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) has spoken. I hope that as part of this debate our colleague, the Conservative Member for Essex-Kent (Mr. Caldwell), who has assisted on a number of important environmental initiatives which have crossed Parties because of the serious problems which exist in the Windsor area, will also feel that it is important to speak on these issues and will make clear his commitment on these concerns.
In discussing this Bill as it has come back from committee, I think we must bear in mind the expectations of Canadians. It is quite clear that their expectations for the environment and the future of our planet are very high. These expectations have been expressed, for example, by the Brundtland Commission report on the environment and development which concluded in April, 1987 that national Governments should establish clear environmental goals and enforce environmental laws, regulations, incentives, and standards on industrial enterprises, and that this should normally be done at the national level with local Governments being empowered to exceed but not to lower national norms.
The Bill before us certainly contains some steps in the right direction, but in studying it one must conclude that it is essentially weak legislation which does not establish that strong national environmental leadership for which Canadians are crying out. For instance, the legislation has not included consideration of some of the most destructive substances that are in use today. Pesticides, for instance, are not regulated, nor are emissions from motor vehicles. I say that as someone from an automotive city. That is something we should be taking leadership on at the national level.

May 2, 1988
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
The Bill does not provide standards of environmental quality. It does not redress the principle that has contributed to our current high levels of pollution, the principle that a substance must be proved harmful before it can be regulated. We need a regulatory tool that requires that substances be proven harmless before they can be used.
The Bill certainly does not incorporate an environmental bill of rights, a bill of rights which would give Canadians a sense of commitment to a healthy environment on the part of the national Government. Canadians have asked the Government for the right to take any polluter to court, for the right to environmental qualilty, and for the right to participate in decision-making with respect to the environment. However, that has not been provided by this Bill.
In fact, this Bill does not advance us beyond the 1970s in terms of environmental legislation. The approach is still a substance by substance one, one that aims to manage toxic chemicals instead of seeking to reduce them. In short, environmental goals are not set out and environmental leadership is not being taken.
Many of us have fought on a series of environmental issues for the last four years of this Government. We have fought a hard-fought battle to try to force the Government to recognize the concerns of Canadians about the environment. The weakness of the legislation and the fact that it takes such small steps forward is not a surprise.
I think, for instance, of the fights which we have had to undertake within our communities of Essex County and Windsor which have continually come up against the brick wall of the Government's unwillingness to respond and act when citizens have demanded action by petition, have requested action of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), and have solicited the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to show some backbone in dealing with the United States. Again and again a brick wall has been met.
We can talk about the blob which was discovered in the St. Clair River which contained a concentration of dioxin such as had never been experienced in our Great Lakes system before. That information would not have come out from the provincial Conservative Government, had it not been for a brave individual who came into my office and talked about the realities which had been discovered and covered up by that provincial Government.
The Government at that stage, with a new Minister of the Environment leading the charge, said: "Let's act, let's get something to happen". In fact, action took place. However, three years later I have learned in discussions with people from Dow Chemicals that there is still coming up from the bottom of the St. Clair River the same toxic material which was there when this originally came to our attention in 1984 and 1985.
The problem has not been solved. There was a great public relations burst by the Minister and $12 million was spent by Dow Chemical, but we did not get a solution to the problem. That is the environmental record of the Government-high public relations and low public performance.
We can talk about mundane things. Members of Parliament from the Windsor area have brought before the Minister of the Environment again and again serious problems which leave thousands of houses in the southern part of Windsor and in parts of Sandwich West with septic tanks and, consequently, leakage into rivers and drainage ditches throughout the community.
What has happened? Has the Government moved? Has it said that it will respond to an urgent problem brought before it? Not a chance. Instead there has been a complete lack of action despite the pressure from myself, my colleague, the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy), and the Member for Windsor West. After looking at the performance of the Government, it has still been necessary to conclude that the Government does not care about that problem.
We can talk about the incinerator, the great Detroit incinerator, which like St. George against the dragon the Minister of the Environment was going to slay. He was going to enforce serious environmental controls on it for the future. It is almost a year and a half ago that the Minister of the Environment went to Windsor and said "We have solved the problem of the Detroit incinerator and do not have to worry about it for the future".
Well, the reality is that the Detroit incinerator continues to go up. There has been no commitment by either the Michigan Government or the City of Detroit to put the latest technology into that incinerator to prevent air coming across the river into Canada which will massively increase the pollution problems in my community.
The Premier of Ontario, that other great white hope, met with the Governor of Michigan, Mr. Blanchard. The Premier said that we were supposed to have an agreement with Michigan with respect to pollution problems. Absolutely not. There was no commitment whatsoever with respect to this very serious problem.
When this problem was first brought before the Minister, he said that it was no problem, that the Government would set up an action group of Members of Parliament from the Windsor area plus representatives from the Ministry itself, and that we would get action. Well, that so-called action group has not met once since the Minister set it up. So much for the real performance of the Government as opposed to its rhetoric. Its public performance in the face of serious problems has been disastrous.
We can say the same thing with respect to the Detroit city airport and its expansion, another environmental problem which will hit much of the City of Windsor and could bring dangerous consequences to people throughout the community.
May 2, 1988

Once again there was no commitment to move, no commitment even to communicate with the United States and convey the concerns of those who live in the community which is to be affected.
Perhaps the most telling, the most damaging, the most obvious dereliction of duty on the part of the Government with respect to the environment in our part of Essex County and Windsor has been with respect to Fermi II. It is over a year since I started raising this question. I put questions to the Government and wrote to both the Minister of the Environment and the Secretary of State for External Affairs indicating the serious problems existing with this reactor which is less than 10 kilometres from Canada. It is very close to population centres in Canada. That nuclear reactor has serious maintenance problems because of its age, even though it has just begun to generate power at 100 per cent capacity. It has serious monitoring problems, as well as serious basic design problems.
When one looks at the record of how it got its license to operate, it is absolutely clear that the wool was pulled over the eyes of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission in the United States. It effectively held back information from that agency which members of the agency subsequently said would have prevented Fermi II from getting its licence. Despite that, the Government is not prepared to take action and tell the American Government that the people of Essex County and those affected by this nuclear reactor have asked for a joint review into what they believe are serious safety problems. The Government has not been prepared to refer the problem to the International Joint Commission.
We met with the International Joint Commission which told us that if it received a reference, it would have tremendous power to probe the problems that exist with this reactor. Yet, it is evident from letters from the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of the Environment that they have consistently told us that they believe the Nuclear Regulatory Commission is the one that should do the job and that Canada has no responsibility for this serious health concern to Canadians.
I must express my disappointment not only at the performance of the federal Government with respect to Fermi II, but also at the performance of the Ontario Government which has been approached but is unwilling to add its voice to the need for a joint review of the safety problems with respect to this nuclear reactor.
That is just a small list of what we have had to face as Members of Parliament from the Windsor and Essex County area in trying to kick the Government into action on the environmental problems affecting our people. While this Bill continues the tradition of great rhetoric, it does not give us any promise of serious, consistent action in the future. We cannot
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
trust a Government which has been so grossly incompetent in the past, as I believe this list of problems clearly shows.

Mr. Speaker, I was particularly interested in my colleague's concerns about the environmental questions affecting his City of Windsor. Has he noted any difference between the actions of the present Government and the former Government?
I recall in 1983 being part of a group with New Democrats from the provincial Legislature of Ontario touring the Windsor and Niagara area. We looked at the Love Canal situation and found a continuing ignorance of the environment, particularly of the effects that toxic substances could have on present and future generations.
Local citizens and environmental groups told us of their frustration because the laws helped polluters and hindered those who were interested in fighting pollution.
I agree with my colleague. This legislation is a lot of sound and fury signifying nothing. Is there any difference between the actions of this Government and the previous Government?

Mr. Speaker, I was not a Member of Parliament during the period of the previous Government. There is a strong desire among those who control the industrial power within our society to deal with the pollution problems in the easiest and least costly way. That desire leads to emissions of serious pollutants into the air. It has lead to emissions of pollutants into the Great Lakes that have resulted in the conclusion that the Great Lakes between Canada and the United States are the most polluted, environmentally toxic area in the world.
On the other side, there are very well intentioned Ministers of the Environment who are not strong enough to have the political leverage over the power centres within their Parties that are so influenced by those large-scale industrial groups. I believe there has always been such a battle. The consequence is that very often Ministers of the Environment, both Conservative and Liberal in the past, had to work very hard to influence their cabinet colleagues.
I recall interviewing Canada's first Minister of the Environment, a Liberal Minister, when he was appointed in 1969-70. He made the point that he had to push very hard to get his cabinet colleagues to move. I suspect that the same is true with the present Minister of the Environment.
I am certain that he truly believed it when he went to Windsor and said the problem with the Detroit incinerator was solved. However, it has not turned out to be the case because people in his Party have been far more concerned with getting a trade deal with the United States than fighting for environmental concerns within this cross border situation.
I think we have a structural problem which can only be confronted if we have first mobilized very strongly public

May 2, 1988
opinion to get a serious and comprehensive change of commitment, so that the environment becomes the number one concern, not an afterthought, not something that brings us a Bill four years after the Government comes to power. What we see in front of us is something which afflicts both Liberal and Conservative Governments. It is something which, frankly, New Democrats would face as well in government. We would need a very strong commitment, not just from our own Party but from people and groups right across this country, in order to bring about a very strong and effective environmental policy. I believe it can be done, but it is going to be a hard fight.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask my hon. friend a short question. We have an important Bill here. I was wondering if the New Democratic Party was going to support it.

Mr. Speaker, I made it clear in my speech that we are always in favour of small steps forward. Unfortunately, small steps forward are not satisfactory to the people of this country. It is not enough to take dainty little steps into the future as this Government is doing. We must-and I am convinced after the next election that it will be done-put in place a pattern of commitment, of boldness, and of serious intent which will give us significant change, a significant move forward under a New Democratic Government, and which will give us a much better commitment to the environment.
The Hon. Member for Davenport on a very short question or comment.

Mr. Speaker, I would briefly like to ask the Hon. Member for Essex Windsor (Mr. Langdon) a question. I know it is difficult for the Member to recognize good initiatives when they take place, when they are taken by a Government whose stripe is not his own, but would he not agree, however, that Ontario has today the toughest environmental laws it has ever had in its history?
The Hon. Member for Essex Windsor on a brief answer, please.

Yes, I very much agree that the previous Conservative Government which was in power for so long did so little that the important steps which were undertaken during the minority Government, with New Democratic Party support, were very crucial to our province and to our future. Unfortunately, since there has been a majority Government elected in Ontario we have seen a slowing down of these initiatives. I think of the Fermi II situation. It is absolutely unforgivable that the Ontario Government has not added its voice as powerfully as it possibly could to those of us from Essex County who are calling for a joint review of safety with respect to this dangerous nuclear reactor being so close to our boundaries.
That concludes the questions and comments. Resuming debate.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity, although there are only four minutes left until the House takes recess, to speak to Bill C-74, allegedly an Act respecting the protection of the environment and of human life and health.
I would have liked to take a more positive stand, if the Bill before the House today had been as strong a piece of legislation as was claimed earlier by the Hon. Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday).
When the Bill was tabled in the House on first reading, the impression was that this Bill had some strong points and that it was an important step towards improving the quality of our environment.
However, after everything that has happened so far and all the so-called consultation, we now have before us a Bill that has very little to show for all this frenzied activity. There are so many fundamental problems connected with the quality of the environment, the environment in which we live, that I think some comments are very much in order on what this Bill contains and, especially, on what it does not contain, in its present form.
When the Minister of the Environment agrees to ask his colleagues for advice on legislation or regulations concerning the environment, I think he is making a big mistake, because there are emergencies when the Minister of the Environment must act without necessarily consulting each of his colleagues to find out what position he should take.
If we consider certain toxic products that are being trucked or shipped across Quebec and across Canada and if we look at the accidents that have happened in recent years, I have serious doubts about the quality of the regulations we had at the time and still have here in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I hope I will have a few minutes more this afternoon to talk about the position taken, for instance, by the Government of Quebec on environmental problems and the kind of action that should be taken very shortly so that the Government of Canada and the governments of the various provinces can introduce environmental legislation that is strong enough to protect the quality of life and the quality of the environment in this country.
Mr. Speaker, you are signaling that I should stop ... [English]

It being one o'clock p.m., I do leave the chair until two o'clock p.m. later this day.
At 1 p.m. the House took recess.

Mr. Speaker, Ontario Environment Minister Jim Bradley quite rightly commented on Saturday that the much heralded Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) special relationship with President Reagan has proven worthless in resolving the acid rain issue. As Mr. Bradley stated, they have come to the end of the line and have nothing to show in the way of acid rain reductions-not one drop.
If Chairman Gorbachev can convince President Reagan to scrap missiles aimed at America's chief enemy, why can the Prime Minister not get the President to stop bombarding America's closest friend with acid rain? Acid rain costs Canada hundreds of millions of dollars a year. Canadian efforts to clean up acid rain are hampered by U.S. inaction.
Mr. Bradley told high school students that half the acid rain deposited in Ontario originates in the United States. No matter what we do, we cannot solve the acid rain problem by ourselves.
Mr. Bradley made his point effectively. When the U.S. administration will understand is another matter.

subtopic: MONTREAL CEREMONY COMMEMORATING BATTLE OF THE ATLANTIC
MONTREAL CEREMONY COMMEMORATING BATTLE OF THE ATLANTIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday afternoon at the Victoria Wharf Clock Tower in the Port of Montreal an important event took place under the auspices of the Canadian Legion Branch 212 of LaSalle.
This highly emotional ceremony was held to commemorate our marine heroes of the Battle of the Atlantic during the last World War. Numerous wreaths were laid at the foot of the monument facing the St. Lawrence River which leads to the sea, by Presidents of different Montreal legion branches, among which was President George Stundon of my own LaSalle branch.
The ceremonial parade was led by our legion members and army cadets. But the highly poignant instant of the commemorative event was when an 88-year old mother of a son lost at sea was invited by the officer in charge to lay flowers in memory of all sons, cousins, uncles, and fathers who gave their lives to safeguard the democratic liberties of our free world.
Lest we forget. Je me souviens.

Mr. Speaker, it is important that the Government, and especially the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), recognize the serious drought threat presently existing in much of western Canada. For example, in the Kamloops area this year's spring run off is 50 per cent below normal. The Thompson River is flowing at 64 per cent of its normal rate. Streams and water-holes are dry or near dry. The Environment and Parks Ministry's hydrology section is predicting drought conditions throughout central British Columbia.
Last year was Kamloops' second driest year on record with only 160 millimetres of precipitation, and the hottest year ever recorded in history.
While cattlemen face the most dire difficulties, other problems are created by drought as well. Fires and drought, unfortunately, go hand in hand. The commercial, native, and sports fisheries are placed at risk. Water fowl habitat is destroyed. Many community reservoirs are near dry. Irrigation districts are forced to cut back on water supply.
On the Prairies many grain farmers are wondering if they should spring seed, since in some regions the soil lacks sufficient moisture for seeds to germinate.
In light of these conditions and the possible drought crisis, the Government should be developing contingency plans which would be implemented quickly if the tragic necessity does arise.

subtopic: BILL C-54-CALL FOR REFERRAL TO COMMITTEE
BILL C-54-CALL FOR REFERRAL TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there has been much public debate about Bill C-54 which amends the Criminal Code relating to pornographic or erotic material. This Bill would serve to prohibit pornography, particularly where children are being depicted in sexual acts, or in cases showing violent pornography and degrading sexual acts against any person.
It is unfortunate that both opposition Parties and some people in the arts community are saying that the Bill is directed at art forms; some librarians have stated that they will have to segregate some books. I believe that these groups have exaggerated a few of the points the Bill, making it seem puritanical. This is just not so. If amendments are needed to clarify the wording it is up to us to let the legislative committee do its work.

May 2, 1988
I call upon the Government and the opposition Parties to let this Bill go through second reading and go to committee in order that this vital piece of legislation can be passed before we break for the summer.

Mr. Speaker, it seems strange that if you are a government employee living in Ottawa or a government employee living in Edmonton, you have different rights. There are more rights for those in Ottawa, and less rights for those in Edmonton. I refer specifically to the issue of child care.
As you are no doubt aware, Mr. Speaker, today we expect the opening of a work site day care in Tunney's Pasture for employees serving the Ottawa area, and at the same time a similar child care operation which was proposed for the opening of Canada Place in Edmonton, scheduled to open in Edmonton next month, has been put on hold.
The child care situation in Edmonton is in limbo because the federal Treasury Board and the Department of Public Works have not got together to put forward the necessary funding. I guess that parents at federal government workplaces in Edmonton must be asking, "What is it that makes federal employees in Ottawa more important than federal employees in Edmonton?"
I would like to say that if the federal Government is serious about encouraging workplace child care, it should put its money where its mouth is and set an example not only in Ottawa but in every area across the country.

Mr. Speaker, it is a tribute to the professionalism and experience of our Armed Forces that once again Canada has been asked by the United Nations to serve in a peace-keeping operation.
This time five Canadian officers are being sent to Afghanistan to monitor, in co-operation with military personnel from other neutral countries, the withdrawal of Soviet troops pursuant to the UN negotiated Geneva agreement.
We wish Lieutenant-Colonel Leslie and his team all possible success with the difficult and possibly dangerous monitoring task to which they have been assigned.

Mr. Speaker, this weekend the President of VIA Rail, Denis De Belleval, said that our rolling stock is the "worst in the world".
It is not exactly a new thing to find out that VIA's transportation system is in shock. People are used to travelling from Thompson to Churchill wearing parkas inside the coaches. That is not only the case in northern Manitoba, but also on the main line. People, including myself, who have taken trains from Winnipeg to Thunder Bay, to Sudbury and on to Ottawa, have woken up each morning frozen because of the antiquated system.
We also have a train system on which tourists who are travelling in this country find that they cannot get accommodation. People who live in small communities in my riding without road access cannot get on a train because there is not adequate equipment.
Prior to the 1984 election the Conservatives promised that there would be new rolling stock in place. That is another broken promise, a promise which results, as the president of VIA Rail says, in us having the worst in the world. What a record. What a broken promise.

subtopic: DESIGNATION OF GRAND FALLS NFLD., AS FORESTRY CAPITAL OF CANADA
DESIGNATION OF GRAND FALLS NFLD., AS FORESTRY CAPITAL OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this week in Canada communities all across the country will be celebrating National Forest Week.
Grand Falls, Newfoundland, is especially honoured this year because it has been named forestry capital of Canada. This designation acknowledges the importance that Grand Falls places on forestry, and helps to focus the attention of all Newfoundlanders on the vital role forestry plays in our economy and our lives. National Forestry Week extends that awareness to include all Canadians.
The forest sector is a cornerstone of the Newfoundland economy, generating direct and indirect employment for 12,300 people. The federal Government is aware of the importance of forestry to this province and is investing $33.6 million in the $48 million Canada-Newfoundland Forest Resource Development Agreement. This week we should all take the opportunity to learn about our most important natural resource, our forests.
May 2, 1988

Mr. Speaker, just 10 kilometres from my constituency the threat of the Fermi II nuclear reactor to Canadians is real. Over 7,500 people have signed petitions against it and all four Members of Parliament from the area have appealed against its operation. Now the Ontario Government has joined us.
I have here a letter from Joan Smith, Ontario Attorney General, to the federal Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) calling for an investigation of these safety concerns. It is unfortunate that the Ontario Government would not go one step further and call for a joint Canadian-U.S. review of Fermi by an independent expert team, but this letter does push the federal Government to move on this issue. So far, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) have been afraid to do so.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: False.
Again and again, they have refused. They must move now for the sake of the hundreds of thousands of Canadians at risk due to the poor maintenance, monitoring and design record of this reactor.

Mr. Speaker, Canada's ambassador to Ethiopia has finally recognized that country's food crisis has a political component. Drought is not its only cause. It never has been, Mr. Speaker. It has always been partly due to the Marxist militaristic oppressive regime of that country. The dictatorial Derg has been determined to turn Ethiopia into a massive collective farm even if that reduces food production. It has spent 46 per cent of its resources on weapons while its people have gone hungry. It is now preventing food supplies from reaching two million people in the rebel held North.
Canada has condemned the use of food supplies as an instrument of political policy. It is time and more than time that we condemned this action in Ethiopia.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lawrence I. O'Neil (Cape Breton Highlands-Canso):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to urge that changes to the Canada Pension Plan disability criteria be made.
The requirement that an applicant be disabled to the point that he or she can do no other type of work now or in the future is too onerous. The fact is that many applicants who, for the purposes of private insurance and provincial programs, are disabled are being told that they are ineligible for benefits under the Canada Pension Plan because they are not disabled. This is very perplexing to these Canadians. To be told by government doctors that they are ineligible is to leave these Canadians with a feeling of injustice.
It is time that the test be changed and the long delays eliminated.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CO-OPERATIVE HOUSING IN METRO TORONTO
APPROVAL OF CO-OPERATIVE HOUSING IN METRO TORONTO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you realize, there is a severe affordable housing crisis in the greater Metropolitan Toronto area. One of the best ways to create affordable housing is to build co-op housing.
Because of that it is particularly distressing to learn that while the affordable housing crisis in Metro has grown progressively more severe the amount of co-op housing approved for Metro by CMHC has steadily declined from 1,182 units in 1981 to 682 units in 1984, to only 126 units in 1987.
What is going on at CMHC? Are they all asleep to reality at CMHC?

subtopic: CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF MINISTRY OF FORESTRY
CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF MINISTRY OF FORESTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as Canadians well know, this is National Forest Week. During National Forest Week we are reminded that the forest sector of the Canadian economy employs 750,000 Canadians. It is the mainstay for over 348 single-industry towns. Indeed, it is a backdrop for tourism and the outdoor recreation industry in Canada.
This might be a good time to remind the Government that it has promised on a number of occasions to bring in a full

May 2, 1988
Oral Questions
Forestry Ministry. A full Ministry of Forestry ought to be announced this week, National Forest Week. I would encourage the Government to take that initiative and to give forestry the due it deserves.

Mr. Speaker, some RCMP personnel and some civil servants live in government owned houses in Banff and Lake Louise. Because of the age of the houses, a "kind" Government ordered a 10 per cent to 15 per cent reduction in the rent. A few months later, actually in early 1988, the renters were advised that income tax would be levied on the amount that the rent had been reduced and, furthermore, that it would be retroactive to January, 1987.
I always thought that income tax was levied on income received, not on money saved through a reduction in rent. But not any more. A bureaucrat in Revenue Canada has informed me that the rent reduction is a tax benefit and the Mounties and the park officials will have to pay income tax on it.
Judging from this, we will soon be paying income tax on the savings we make by buying at a sale, and even on the nickel that is deducted by a kind candy maker. Heaven help us!

Mr. Speaker, a few weeks ago, Premier Peterson initiated the largest, most cynical tax grab in Ontario's enduring memory. In order to offset some bad publicity, Peterson said that the tax increase was to pay for the rise in cost of health care. However, the opposite is true.
The financial outlook for public hospitals, of which 50 per cent are operating in the red, is bleak, and they will receive nothing. Hospital funding remains at last year's figure of 6.9 per cent, of which 4.4 per cent represents across-the-board increases for inflation. Hospitals have been forced to impose a virtual freeze on programs and services and on appointments of badly needed medical specialists to staff.
With our aging population, and serious medical problems such as AIDS looming on the horizon, our public hospitals must have the capability to meet the needs of the community. It is obvious that the Peterson Budget was only an excuse to gouge the taxpayer while jeopardizing the future health of the population.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. As everybody knows, today is the deadline for filing personal income tax returns.
Could the Minister of Finance explain to the House why personal income tax, not corporate taxes but the taxes of average Canadians, totals $26.7 billion more this year than in 1984 when his Government came to power?
During the last election campaign the Conservatives, and with them the Minister, promised they would not increase taxes.
Will the Minister of Finance explain to the House and to Canadians why he violated this election promise by taking $26.7 billion out of the pockets of average Canadian families?

Mr. Speaker, I think it is very important to understand that 24 per cent of the increase in revenue of the Government of Canada is due to the increase in our economic growth rate.
It is true that we have increased taxes as a result of budgetary decisions, but 24 per cent of the increase is a result of economic growth and the Government's policies, which have led to higher employment. We have 1,200,000 more jobs in Canada and an economy whose growth rate is the best among the G-7 countries.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister finally recognized that he has increased taxes between the 1984 return and the 1987 return which Canadians are forced to file, and by $26.7 billion.
You're wrong. You correct that. That's absolutely wrong.
Wait a minute.
That is wrong.

speechtext: While there may be some disagreement, I would ask the Hon. Minister to-
Quit distorting things like that.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would ask the Hon. Minister to wait until he responds, and if there is a disagreement the Hon. Minister can
May 2, 1988

certainly comment upon it. I would ask the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition to put his question.

Mr. Speaker, let me be precise so that the Minister can relax. I can understand why he is a little raw today when people are paying their taxes right across the country.
He has admitted to raising taxes. He has not admitted the figure that I cited. However, I will recite again that the increase between the 1984 tax return and the 1987 tax return for individual income tax is $26.7 billion.
Let us not even talk about the 77 per cent increase in sales taxes under this Government. Let us talk about what happens to the income tax of the ordinary Canadian family after four Budgets of this Minister, after all the surtaxes, after the deindexation, and after the so-called tax reform.
Will the Minister explain why, even after tax reform, a Canadian family with an income of $25,000 a year will be paying $390 more in income tax than it paid in 1984, and why a family with an income of $40,000 a year will be paying $840 a year more in income tax than in 1984, while a family with an income of $120,000 a year will be paying $3,570 less than in 1984? Is that the Minister's idea of tax fairness?

Mr. Speaker, I would have a bit more respect for the Leader of the Opposition if he did not completely distort what I said in an answer just a minute before he made the comment which he did. He knows perfectly well that his statement that $26 billion is a result of tax increases is a total distortion. He would have more respect from the people of Canada, and possibly the people in his caucus, if he would recognize that that sort of distortion should not be used in the House of Commons in the way in which he just has used it.
If his memory is that short, allow me to repeat for him that more than 80 per cent of the increase in the revenues of the Government of Canada over that period of time is because of growth in the economy and the increase in the number of jobs that have been created. One million two hundred thousand jobs have been created. More people are paying tax. The revenues have gone up because people are working.
Another reason the revenues of the Government of Canada have gone up is that we have the best growth record of the G-7 nations.
Yes, we have increased taxes. I have never made any secret of that.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: You promised you wouldn't

Allow me to make just one more comment, Mr. Speaker. I know you are getting anxious to get up.
