Yes, we have raised taxes, but that is simply because of the huge-and I repeat, huge-fiscal problem that we inherited in 1984.

Mr. Speaker, the figures I am reciting are derived from the statistics of the Minister's own Department reinforced by independent agencies such as the Institute of Public Policy. I would be glad to furnish him with support for every number I have raised here in the House.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is no wonder that Canadians are upset about paying their taxes today and over the weekend. They have every right to be mad. Ninety-nine per cent of Canadians are paying more in total taxes-I am talking about income tax, sales and excise taxes, and so on-than they were paying in 1984 when the Government came into power after it had said that it would not raise taxes.
Only one per cent of Canadians are paying less in tax. That one per cent of Canadians consists of those whose income is more than $117,000 a year. Those happen to be the facts.
Will the Minister explain why someone making $17,000 a year is paying more in taxes, while the person making $117,000 a year is paying less in taxes since he came to power?

Mr. Speaker, with the way the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition, a former Finance Minister, is playing with figures today, I will not comment on any numbers that he gave. He said that $26 billion is totally because of tax increases. Is that what the Hon. Member is saying?
They are paying more in taxes by $26.8 billion.
Is the Hon. Member saying that is totally because of tax increases?
I am saying that was the result of his four Budgets-
Oh, oh!

There you have it, Mr. Speaker. That is the distortion. The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition is playing to the television cameras, distorting the numbers out of all reason. He wonders why I do not answer his questions. It is because he is asking questions in a way that has been quite distorted. He knows perfectly well that the reason why people are paying more taxes-

Because you increased them.

May 2, 1988
Oral Questions
-is because their income is up. Their income is up because we have a healthy economy. Do not give me all these distortions.

subsubtopic: THREAT OF DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture. Western Canadian farmers are facing the worst drought in a century, with the lowest rainfalls and precipitation since 1889. Topsoil is blowing in many areas of the Prairies and dug-outs are dry, even with the spring run-off which was practically nil.
What action will the Government take to assist these farmers who are facing the worst drought in one hundred years?

subsubtopic: THREAT OF DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that question was posed to me by one of the members of caucus last week. I indicated in response to his question that indeed the potential for a drought in Western Canada is very high. In fact we are advised by PFRA officials who are in the field that moisture levels are perhaps at a forty-year low. It is potentially very serious.
As one producer indicated just a few days ago, we have not lost a crop in April yet. We must be hopeful that mother nature will look favourably upon us, but the Hon. Member should take some satisfaction in the fact that since the latter part of February and first part of March there has been a federal-provincial and producer task force looking at a number of options. It will continue to do its work. Hopefully we will get moisture. In fact I am advised by my Parliamentary Secretary that most parts of Manitoba received considerable rainfall last night.

Mr. Speaker, when will the Government give some kind of commitment to western farmers that it will provide assistance in this national emergency? The Government of Alberta has already committed some S20 million. When will the Government, which has already cut the PFRA budget drastically in the last number of years, give a total and complete commitment to the prairie provinces? He knows that the disaster is beyond Alberta and affects much of Saskatchewan as well.

Mr. Speaker, if anyone wants to take the time to examine the record of how this Government has responded positively in previous situations, that person should take some comfort with respect to our willingness to accept our responsibility in the future.
Let me inform the Hon. Member that when the Prime Minister appeared before the Outlook Conference in the first part of December, he gave a commitment of some $75 million in the area of soil and water conservation, to be matched by the provinces. subsubtopic: CHILDREN IN POVERTY-AGENDA FOR FIRST MINISTERS' MEETING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. It concerns the tragedy of child poverty. Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It concerns his statement in the House last Friday in answer to a question, wanting credit for a so-called win with regard to NOx emissions. If he got the American Government to agree to a reduction in NOx emissions we would call it a win, and we would give him credit for it.
I hope that today he will be specific about what is in this win. Are there real reductions to which the American Government has agreed? Or does he consider a win to be merely the fact that the Americans have agreed to keep on talking?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the change in Geneva is very substantive. There were two proposals seriously considered by 34 countries during negotiations.
The first would have seen any previous year, not just 1987, as the baseline on which the Americans, among other countries, could calculate the extent to which they met their obligations under the treaty. The Americans, could have chosen 1978, which was their highest year of production of nitrogen oxides, which in turn would have meant that it would have been that much easier for them to meet their obligations. We have eliminated the clause "any previous year".
The second proposal concerned a provision that would have enabled the Americans and other countries, too, to credit reductions in previous years against any future reductions they would be required to make under the protocol. We have removed that provision as well.
It is a double win for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, if indeed the Americans are agreeing to that, then that would be a very significant step.
Will the Minister confirm that this protocol will go ahead without American agreement and that these really crucial matters are still left to bilateral talks? Will he confirm specifically whether or not have the Americans have agreed to get rid of the "any year" provision? Have the Americans agreed to at least a freeze? Are the Americans prepared to go ahead with stated objectives for reductions in NOx emissions?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the short answer is that all the prospective signatory countries have returned to their respective jurisdictions to consult their Governments with a view to coming back to the table on July 1, 1988, a few months hence, to tell the other partners the extent to which they can go along with the protocol as drafted.
We will not know, presumably until then, or some time before the first of July, what the final position of the United States might be. I am hopeful.
However, as the Prime Minister indicated in connection with Canada-U.S. negotiations in Washington, short of pointing a cannon at Washington, what more can we do? We have put our case forcefully to the Americans, and to the world community. I think we have performed a service to the country in doing so.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Communications. It concerns the lack of a full English language service in New Brunswick, the only province in Canada without a CBC owned and operated television service.
Last month officials told the Premier of New Brunswick that the corporation could not find the $10 million to $20 million needed to give New Brunswick this full service. Yet, two weeks later, $220 million was found for equipment for a new broadcast centre.
How can the Minister explain to the Premier and the people of New Brunswick that, on the one hand, they can find up to $380 million for a new broadcast centre and, on the other hand, they cannot find $10 million to $20 million to give a full CBC service to New Brunswickers? Mr. Speaker, I simply want to indicate to the Deputy House Leader that we appreciate the advance notice earlier today, that the Government intended to change the order of business and get on dealing with the western diversification Bill.
I agree with the Minister of State that the environmental protection legislation presently before the House is very important. While it is our intention to support that legislation as enthusiastically as we can, there are a number of points we feel ought to be made before the Bill leaves the House. Those will be done quickly, expeditiously, and in a very business-like way as soon as possible.

The House resumed from Friday, April 29, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mulroney that Bill C-113, an Act to promote the development and diversification of the economy of western Canada, to establish the Department of Western Economic Diversification and to make consequential amendments to other Acts, be read the third time and passed, and the motion of Mr. Hawkes:
That this question be now put.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to finish my remarks on the western diversification legislation. I should point out to those watching today that again we have a situation where the Government has changed the legislation before the House in a very haphazard manner.
One hour prior to this debate we were still debating Bill C-74, the environmental legislation. Now we are back to debating the western diversification Bill. It is obvious that the Government is running out of time in this legislative session. It knows its legislative program is in trouble. The Government has yet to start debate on free trade and to introduce legislation on Air Canada. The Government knows that legislatively its back is to the wall. As a result, we have the unusual situation where we deal with one piece of legislation in the morning and a different piece is dragged into the House for the afternoon. Every time there is a piece of legislation on the Order Paper, the Government attempts to extend the hours of the House. It moves to prevent legitimate amendments in the House.
Western Economic Diversification Act
This is a very difficult situation for those Members who are scheduled to speak and so engage in legitimate debate. There is absolutely no way we can believe the Government when it says what the Orders of the Day are or what the Business of the House will be for the next day.
The House has found it almost impossible to have a legislative timetable, because the Government has been unable to get its act together. It recognizes now, with two months left and the number of Opposition Days guaranteed by the rules of the House, that it will have a problem. The Government's way of dealing with that is not to sit down and negotiate with the opposition Parties in trying to come up with a timetable to see which pieces of legislation can be dealt with. The Government's approach is a bluster approach. The Government announces on Thursday what the Business of the House will be for the following week, yet a few hours later changes its mind. Even before Thursday is over there is a change with regard to Friday.
On Friday the Government announced that we would be dealing with the western diversification legislation and on Monday morning, an hour before the House sat, we found out that we were dealing with the environmental protection legislation. We went through the morning with that piece of legislation and made our plans for the afternoon. Just before Question Period started today we were told by the Minister of State (Mr. Lewis) that we would be back to debating the western diversification Bill.
These procedures tell us that the Government is out of control and that the Government is unable to plan a legislative timetable. It is hoping to catch the Opposition napping. The Government wants to ram through some pieces of legislation quickly in order to see if it can recapture some time. If it is following those tactics, the Government should realize that the probability of co-operation from the Opposition will diminish.
If our critics do not have notice and if members in Standing Committees are pulled out of those committees without notice, one cannot expect opposition Members to co-operate with the Government. The Government should realize that. It should stop playing this kind of poker game by dealing cards and, if it does not like the way the cards fall, taking them back and dealing them again. That is what is happening.
There are enough Members on the government side who sat in opposition when the Liberals tried the same tricks in the past to know that members of the Opposition do not like it. It makes it impossible to work and do the types of things that are necessary as a Member of Parliament and as a member on a committee, if the Government continues to change legislation the way it has.
I was particularly upset when the Parliamentary Secretary rose on Friday and moved the previous question on the issue of western diversification. This is an issue which affects all parts of the West and on which many Members of the House from western Canada have not had an opportunity to speak. It was forced through the House quickly at second reading stage.

Western Economic Diversification Act
When it went to committee, the Government refused to allow the committee to travel to western Canada, even though the committee studying a similar piece of legislation affecting Atlantic Canada was allowed to travel.
As I said on Friday in the few moments that I had to speak then, there are people in western Canada who would like to speak on this legislation. There are people who have various opinions on this legislation. They have ideas of their own on how the West should develop and what role the federal Government should be taking in supporting that development and diversification. Those people cannot all afford to come to Ottawa. By its very nature, the House of Commons will not pay for the transportation of all those groups to Ottawa.
This Bill is a regional Bill and it should have been taken to the region so that people from Edmonton, Calgary, Red Deer, Kamloops, Prince George, Vancouver, Victoria, and the smaller communities could make presentations. The same is true for the people of the Provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. The people from those provinces would have liked to have spoken on western diversification, but they were denied the opportunity to do so.
When the Parliamentary Secretary, a Member from Calgary, rose to move the previous question and, by doing so, limited debate on this matter, I was appalled. First we were denied the opportunity to travel to the West, and now we have been denied the opportunity to express fully our concerns with regard to this legislation.
I am not the only one with these concerns. I could quote the remarks of all sorts of groups that have concerns with this legislation. I am not just talking about those groups that have traditionally supported the New Democratic Party or the CCF. I am not talking strictly of the co-operative movement, the labour movement, or some of the other groups that are famous for having left-wing, co-operative approaches to issues. I can also quote the remarks of other groups from western Canada that are concerned with the format, the concept, and the fact that decision making will not really take place in the West. These groups are concerned that there may not be a coordination of over-all government policy within the structure developed by the Government.
The Canadian Federation of Independent Business has suggested that this measure might be a political slush fund, and if it is not a political slush fund, that it might be a bureaucratic slush fund. The Federation has said that it is a narrow, highly centralized approach to diversification with a continued emphasis on megaprojects. The Federation calls it a confusing black box lacking clear criteria or policy direction and has said that it is on a collision course with a myriad of client groups who will inevitably see thousands of applications rejected and thousands of hopes dashed. That is what a group supported by small business is saying about the Western Diversification Fund.
The Federation goes on to make some remarks comparing this measure to the Western Development Fund, what I called the phantom fund of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). The previous Liberal Government promised $4 billion to the West and that was reduced to $2 billion and then disappeared altogether.
I realize that my time is up. I realize that that is a direct consequence of the Government's measure to restrict debate on this very important matter and that it points out the problem with the approach this Government has taken to western diversification. It is not only refusing to listen to the people of the West, but it is restricting the ability of western MPs to speak on this very important matter.

Madam Speaker, in previous attempts at the diversification of the West or of other regions, the legislation has given Departments including DREE and DRIE responsibility for the co-ordination of the efforts of other major Departments such as Finance, Transport, and Health and Welfare. These Departments have co-ordinated efforts to develop programs which would substantially affect the region being diversified. I wonder if the Hon. Member could give us some indication of whether or not he sees something like that as being possible.

Madam Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) for his question. I believe that it is a very important question. It is something that concerns all of us.
The Macdonald Royal Commission on the economy discussed the co-ordination role of DREE, which was supposed to have acted as a co-ordinator with the other federal Departments. Its report indicated that a major federal concern was that DREE was not proving to be very effective in co-ordinating and integrating the activities of other line Departments, and that the line Departments felt relatively little need to pay much attention to regional concerns. As someone who was the DREE critic in those days and who has had an opportunity to see some multidepartmental approaches in northern Manitoba and other places, I recognize that the co-ordinating role will not happen if we simply set up a little agency in Atlantic Canada with a limited political clout and a different agency responsible to a different Minister in western Canada, again with limited political clout. There is no over-all thrust.
I must agree with the Canadian Federation of Independent Business which is very critical of the approach that is being taken. With the new Atlantic agency and the Western Diversification Fund, political motivation and back room deals will be the way decisions will be made. That is a problem. When we see thousands of applications coming from western Canada and only a few being accepted, and some being accepted during provincial election campaigns, we must be skeptical and wonder what the decision-making process is all about. I am very skeptical.

Specifically in answer to the question asked by the Hon. Member for Prince Albert, I believe that the only way there can be an effective co-ordinating role is if there is direct accountability to a Department like the one DREE used to be before the Liberals dismantled it. There must be a responsibility written into the legislation so that various programs will be funnelled through DREE, not just when someone thinks it is necessary or a good idea but as a requirement so that when development is taking place in western Canada, decisions are made in Ottawa, and that is just as important.
Decisions made in Ottawa affect the regions, and I am referring to decisions like the Air Canada-Airbus decision, the CF-18 decision, and a number of other decisions which seem to be made for certain political reasons with no regard for what is happening or for what negative effect it will have. We must see that some second thought is given, and that is what we are not seeing at this time.
I believe that the lack of any clear authority in this legislation means that the diversification agency will have no role over the line Departments and that they will continue, as happened under the Liberal Government, to ignore any role for regional development.

Madam Speaker, as my hon. colleague from Churchill has indicated, one of the very important roles which the Western Diversification Office ought to take on is to be an advocate for western Canada-western Canadian business, western Canadian industry, and western Canadians.
We all remember the CF-18 decision. All the experts said that Bristol Aerospace in Winnipeg should carry on the maintenance of those fighter jets, but the decision was made that the maintenance would go to Montreal. The Member also mentioned Air Canada's pending decision on the Airbus, which would again result in a significant decrease in the maintenance program in Manitoba.
I want to ask the Member about the kaon project. The Member is well aware that the kaon project is a supportive development for the TRIUMF project in British Columbia. British Columbians, particularly the scientists at the University of British Columbia, are very proud of the contribution which that has made to particle science, particularly particle physics. We now have a chance to make this into a world-class scientific project, a leading scientific project in the world. However, it requires a commitment from the federal Government.
Does the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) consider this to be a legitimate role for the Western Diversification Office to play? Does he think it should be an advocate to ensure that westerners, western Canada, and specifically a western university, be the home of a world-class scientific project, the kaon project or the TRIUMF project? This would be in line with the decision of the federal Government to support the space agency and set aside $1.2 billion in scientific
Western Economic Diversification Act
research for that agency which will be done, by and large, in eastern Canadian universities. Does the Hon. Member for Churchill consider this a legitimate role for the Western Diversification Office to play?

Madam Speaker, that is a very interesting question. It points out the problem we have with the legislation and with the way the Government acts. This appears to be a very good project in western Canada which is not being favoured by the Minister responsible. We thought that the Western Diversification Office was co-ordinating development in western Canada. Rather, the Minister, acting by himself, is saying that the Government will probably not sponsor the project.
Were the people at the Western Diversification Office even consulted? We do not know whether they were or not. Was the Minister responsible for western diversification consulted on this decision? Again, we do not know whether or not he was consulted. Was a report made on the merits for western Canada of this project going forward? If so, what were the benefits to the West, and what were some of the negative aspects involved in this decision? Again, we do not know.
When we see important decisions relating to research and scientific and technological study and improvements being turned down in western Canada, we have to wonder whether the Western Diversification Office had any role whatsoever in the decision.
How do you develop co-ordination of various government programs in the West if major decisions are being made by one Minister acting alone, even though they have a fundamental effect on the development of western Canada? Although the money and the programs are needed, the Western Diversification Fund will not help the West unless there is an over-all coordinating role and if they continue to ignore what is happening in the communities and the suggestions of people in the regions.

Madam Speaker, I am happy to have a chance to speak on Bill C-113 because it is a very important Bill in western Canada. We feel western Canada is facing the most difficult time in its history, not only because of the dramatic downturn in oil prices in 1986 which plunged the prices to a level at it is simply not feasible to operate many of the new projects which we would like to see developed in the tar sands and heavy oils, but because the cash flow generated puts a lot of small operators into a serious position.
Government Members are, of course, always very critical of previous government programs with regard to energy. However, it is clear that the Western Accord did not provide for the downturn which we saw in energy prices in 1986. The prices are still hovering at $16 to $17 per barrel. It is my understanding that the economic incentive provided under CEDIP for the past year is going to be phased out as well for oil and gas exploration. Of course, any program under the Western

May 2, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
Economic Diversification Program is all government assistance. Therefore, when programs like CEDIP are phased out we must ask whether this new program takes its place. Of course it does not. It is an entirely different kind of program for an entirely different number of activities.
In addition to CEDIP being phased out, we are seeing the earned depletion allowance being phased out which has provided $600 million or $700 million for mineral exploration and development in the past three or four years. Of course the new program under the Western Economic Diversification Office does not take its place. As a matter of fact it is much smaller. It involves some $60 million a year for each of the four western provinces.
A program which has been instrumental in developing new mines in northern Manitoba and other areas of the West is being phased out at the same time, and the net result is less incentive for exploration and development in the mineral and oil and gas industries, and this at a time when the economy of the West is generally down.
We must look at the program which has been put in place because, even though the legislation has not been passed, there is enabling legislation for departmental reorganization and establishment and grants are being given under the Western Economic Diversification Office. We must look at the programs and grants which have been established.
I had an opportunity to hear some of the witnesses before the committee. One of the most penetrating and decisive descriptions put to the committee was put forward by Dennis Young, the President of the Single-Industry Towns Association He put the argument forward that we should be working more toward developing small industries in individual communities. From the experience I have had in my district, I have been very impressed with programs like the business development centres under the Department of Employment and Immigration. While that program exists in some communities in the West, it does not apply to many areas. Programs under this legislation will not provide that kind of assistance.
Under the Business Development Centres Program, a small amount of money is provided as an incentive for the operation of the Economic Development Corporation. Funds amounting to $275,000 per year are provided at that level.
The funds that are provided for incentives in my area take the form of a loan at regular commercial rates of interest of 11 per cent or 12 per cent. It is amazing that in my constituency, businesses have been able to create some 30 or 40 jobs with capital funds of $275,000 per year. This is not done by large manufacturing concerns or through megaprojects, but with small community-based projects that are expanding businesses. This program provides funds strictly on a loan basis.
A number of witnesses made the argument that this type of program will deliver more effective economic development on a
more sound basis than the present program. I hope that the Government will consider it because it is a valid criticism.
The Single Industry Towns Association points out that most of the grants go to the large cities. I assume that these grants will continue to go to large cities in the West, which perhaps are already more diversified and successful in attracting new business than the rural towns and villages throughout the Prairies which have difficulty in attracting new business.
The Government should consider this concern because it is a very valid criticism. This problem has been overcome in many communities with the use of the Business Development Centres Program under the Department of Employment and Immigration.
Unfortunately, only a limited number of these projects have been approved across the country, and the Western Diversification Program does not provide funding.
Prairie communities have been facing a downturn in the price of oil and natural gas since 1986. They are also suffering from extremely low grain prices. Bill C-113 is not adequate to cope with the dramatic events that are taking place at the international level. The U.S.-European Economic Community trade war is resulting in dramatically reduced property values on farms throughout the West.
I do not believe the economic fall out of this has been fully appreciated. While the report will not be out for another two months, we hear that the Farm Credit Corporation is facing the loss of $500 million to $1 billion. The full impact of this situation has not been investigated, nor has a program been established to deal with the problem.
The Agriculture Committee has been studying agriculture throughout Canada, but clearly the Prairies are facing the greatest challenge in the face of a reduction in the value of commodities, especially grains and oil seeds, and the consequent reduction of farm property values. As farmers lose their equity, their position of stability is being challenged.
Furthermore, many parts of the southern half of Alberta and Saskatchewan are facing a drought situation. Slews are dried up, for the first time in memory, and the dug-outs used to water cattle are dry. Dust storms are blowing away the top soil.
Today I asked the Minister when a program would be announced and what would be the Government's commitment. Alberta has already made a commitment of some $20 million for expanding dug-outs for water supply, for developing new wells and pumping systems. If the situation continues, the Government will have to make a commitment.
It is unfortunate that the Government cut back the budget of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Administration which has provided assistance for the development of water supplies and so on in the past. The budget has been cut to $64 million from some $150 million a few years ago.

Western Canada is facing a difficult time. We are concerned about whether this western diversification office is the proper mechanism to cope with the kind of economic diversification we really need, not only in western Canada, which depends on one or two major resource commodities, but in other parts of the country which face the same kind of difficulties.
The decline of the rural community as a result of lack of funding for useful programs has been exacerbated by the policy not to replace the postmasters who leave rural post offices. Some 5,000 rural post offices are under the gun, along with some 90,000 jobs as a result of that policy. Rural Canadians can only hope that their postmaster will not have to retire in the near future.
Rural communities also require infrastructure, including the replacement of streets, sewers and water works systems. This western diversification program will not provide that important infrastructure for these rural communities.
The Canadian Municipal Association put forward a program a couple of years ago. It stated that over five years it would need a $15 billion program to upgrade rural community infrastructure across the country. That program would have provided $1 billion from the federal Government, $1 billion from the provincial Government and a similar amount from the municipalities across Canada. Unfortunately, under the rural Economic Diversification Program, no funding will be provided for municipal infrastructure. That is unfortunate because various groups that came before the committee complained that not only are the grants going mostly to urban centres across the Prairies but there is very little help for the small towns and communities and no municipal infrastructure is provided under this program. So there are a number of problems that just do not seem to be resolved under this Western Economic Diversification Program.
We are also concerned about the program for railway rehabilitation for western Canada which is essential for the transportation of grain, especially in branch lines. It appears at the present time that this billion dollar program is going to be wound up next year with about $125 million left in the program which will not be made available to do that essential upgrading. Clearly this is a breach of the trust of western communities and the western grain industry. That commitment should be honoured by the Government.
When we talk about $1.2 billion over five years, it sounds like a lot of money, but when we break it down to four provinces per year, we are looking at some $60 million per year. We see the Government phasing out the CIDA program for exploration and development in oil and gas. We see the earned depletion allowance phased out for exploration and development in mining. We see $125 million in the Railway Rehabilitation Program which is not being spent. We see the cut-back in funding for postal services and we see the cut-
Western Economic Diversification Act
backs in the community colleges which are essential for the training and upgrading of our young people. That cut-back involves 40 per cent during the last three or four years. We see a massive number of cut-backs which are not compensated for under this program of western diversification. So I think those are very important concerns which should be addressed.
It is not clear, for instance, with the phasing out of the IDRP program, if the funding provided there is balanced and is the same amount of money as in the Western Economic Diversification Program. Although the delivery mechanism is a little different, there are regional offices, which is an advantage. Is there any net increase in the money for regional development? It is not very clear just what the increase is under any of these programs. Those are some of the concerns I see.
I could go on to talk about the softwood lumber export tax which in British Columbia has been transferred from an export tax to a stumpage charge. For one company alone in Prince George, British Columbia, the stumpage charge went from $6.2 million to $19 million a year when that tax was transferred. That is the kind of problem many rural communities will face in the British Columbia area under the transfer to a new stumpage charge from the export tax charge. So I think there are a number of issues that need to be addressed and considered before this legislation is passed and put into effect.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to both the previous speaker and the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster). I think some things have to be clarified. I would like to ask this question; how can the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy), for example, say with candour that the Government refused to allow the committee to travel when there was no request for the committee to travel? It is unfortunate we are hearing these kinds of things during debate on a very important Bill.
The Hon. Member also said the Government refused to hear witnesses, but the committee heard three witnesses put forward by the New Democratic Party. There was a question on delay in committee, and that is why it was brought back. I would like to ask the Hon. Member for Algoma, who indicated that it was a slush fund and that there were questions to be asked, how he can indicate this when there are basically 58 Progressive Conservative ridings in western Canada and it is going to be very difficult for programs to be approved under the Western Economic Diversification Program if they are not approved in some of the Conservative ridings? How does the Hon. Member square that?

With respect to the Government providing witnesses, there was a terrible battle to get any witnesses before the committee, even the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. It had prepared quite an important paper on the subject and we had a great battle to get it accepted as a witness. A number of witnesses were proposed by the New Democratic Party. Although the Member says three of them were allowed by the Government to attend the

May 2, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
committee hearings, practically none of the witnesses proposed by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), were permitted to appear before the committee. For instance, Dr. Michael Percy, past Director of the Western Centre for Economic Research, University of Alberta, was not permitted to appear. Mr. Ed Guest, Executive Director of the Port of Churchill Development Board was not permitted to appear. Chief Rodney Spence, Nelson House Band, Nelson House, Manitoba, was not permitted to appear. There is a report coming out fairly soon which, I understand, has been prepared by Mr. Michael Decter, a consultant to the Economic Council of Canada, who was not permitted to appear.
I think it is totally understandable that the Hon. Member for the New Democratic Party said that committees never travelled because government Members would not permit it. There is no question about that. There was no agreement even to have any witnesses appear.
When the Hon. Member talks about concern for the funds being used as a slush fund, that is exactly what the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, in its submission to the Minister responsible for economic diversification, said on February 12. On the first page of the executive summary it states with respect to the program, that its enthusiasm has been tempered by growing concern that the western diversification initiative is degenerating into at least one of the following. It then lists the following items.
It states that it is degenerating into a political slush fund to support vulnerable constituencies, lure in big business, or bail out obsolete industries in the hope of gaining short-term political profile. It is not members of the Opposition who are expressing concern about this initiative, it is the Canadian Federation of Independent Business which is expressing the concern that the fund would be used as a slush fund.
Its second concern also refers to a slush fund. It states that it would be a bureaucratic slush fund available for other line Departments and Ministers to raid in lieu of other national programs that should have their fair share spent in the West.
There are two aspects to the slush fund about which the Federation is concerned. The first is that it is a political slush fund for PC candidates who are in trouble in their own ridings, or their big business friends who are in trouble with obsolete industries or industries which are failing. The second concern with regard to the slush fund approach is that it may become a bureaucratic slush fund. The concern that this will be a slush fund is well documented by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business.

Mr. Speaker, I have probably not been more upset than I am today as we are talking about this legislation when Members talk about the process that was used. I want to point out that I was a member of the legislative committee which studied this matter. When we studied the Bill clause by clause a request was made for a list of witnesses to come forward. There was a large list submitted by the Liberal

Member on the committee, and a somewhat watered-down list was received from the New Democratic Member.
Members indicated during the committee that these people had actually requested to appear before the committee. On checking that out we found that they did not request to appear before the committee, but that the request was being orchestrated by the Liberal member on the committee and by the New Democratic member on the committee strictly as a delaying tactic to keep the legislation in committee. In this way it would not be brought into the House and passed, and western diversification could not start to work in western Canada.
The Canadian Federation of Independent Business, for example, was telephoned by the Chairman of the committee who said: "Are you requesting to come before us?" They said that they were not. He then asked: "Do you want to appear before us?" They said: "We really do not want to appear before the committee. If you request us to do so, we will". The Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) by his own words today in debate said that they appeared "at our insistence". That is exactly it. We can bring anyone to a legislative committee as a witness if we want to do it at our insistence. I do not think that that is fair. It is really another way that Members on the other side are trying to delay this Bill, as they have been trying to delay legislation in this House for the past month. They know that people in western Canada are waiting for the legislation. They say one thing out in western Canada and then when the legislation is to be put through which will help individuals, firms and employment in western Canada what do they do? They delay, delay, delay. It is very unfair that they do that. It is very unfair that they present these meaningless arguments that they have put forward to try to justify their position of delay. I will not accept that.
There is another question that came up in debate today. It is one that I resent most sincerely. Members opposite said that the committee was not allowed to travel. The committee did not make a request to travel.

There was never a request to travel before the committee. The subject was never even discussed in committee. It was not a matter of who controlled the committee. It was never brought up in committee. The request was never made.
I am tired of these delaying tactics. Therefore, I would like to put before the House the following motion:
That the House continue to sit beyond the ordinary hour of daily adjournment for the purpose of continuing consideration of third reading of Bill C-113, an Act to promote the development and diversification of the economy of western Canada, to establish the Department of Western Economic Diversification and to make consequential amendments to other Acts.

Shame!

May 2, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Madam Speaker, please tell me how one can ask questions of someone who did not make a speech of any substance of any kind? How can a Minister ask questions of a back-bench Member?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The Minister of Fisheries has the floor on a question or comment.

I wanted to receive an indication from the Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields), who has been very close to the delivery of the western diversification initiative these past several months, whether he has some examples to illustrate the manner in which this very important program is bringing benefit to the four western provinces.
It has been some time now since the office was opened in Edmonton, and there are now sub-offices in all four of the provinces. I think the House would be interested to learn the extent to which these initiatives are bringing benefit to the various sectors of the economy of western Canada, and in particular to achieve the objective, which is to diversify the economy of western Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
I am very happy to have an opportunity to answer the very intelligent question put forward.
One of the things that people in Canada should be made aware of, and particularly the people in western Canada, is that for the first time in the history of this country a full federal Department with a Deputy Minister will be headquartered, not in Ottawa, but in western Canada. The place chosen for the headquarters of this very important Western Economic Diversification Department is Edmonton, and there are suboffices in every province in western Canada.
We talked about the delay in getting the program operational in western Canada. The delay is owing to the fact that we are waiting for the legislation. I hope that it has been noticed that when we attempted to limit debate to today, the NDP and the Liberals stood up en masse, rushing in from the back rooms, and rushing in breathlessly from their offices to defeat that motion in order that they can delay, in exactly the same way that they had been delaying it in committee by asking questions on trivial matters.
Who rang the bells for two weeks in the House? Which Party was that? What a short memory.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
The Member opposite asked who rang the bells in this House for over two weeks. I am happy to say it was the Conservative Members of the Opposition because of the National Energy Program that was being rammed down our throats. It was an ominous energy Bill with the National Energy Program. The NDP and Liberal Members wanted to perpetrate it on western Canada and kill the economy of western Canada. They eventually succeeded in doing that. That is why the bells were rung, because we were trying to protect the interests of western Canada.
Today the NDP and Liberal Members are trying to destroy the interests of western Canada, because they are delaying and delaying. The people in western Canada will not stand for the type of shenanigans that the Liberals and the NDP Members are using today in delaying this western diversification Bill that means so much to western Canadians from all walks of life.
I hope that the people in western Canada will recognize the tomfoolery that is going on across the floor. I would ask the NDP and the Liberals why they are so against western Canada and constantly fighting against western Canada in this House, and then returning to their ridings in western Canada and saying that they are standing up for western Canada, because they truly are not.

I wish to make a comment and ask my friend, the Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields), a question. He was supposed to explain the initiatives approved by the Government's Western Diversification Office that would diversify the economy of western Canada. I notice that he failed to do that in his response to my hon. friend, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon).
The Hon. Member will be aware of a recent proposal put forward by the Thompson Nicola Manufacturers Association. This association was formed two years ago to co-ordinate the efforts of the manufacturing sector in British Columbia. This association in British Columbia represents 500 different manufacturers. It wanted $40,000 from the Western Diversification Office to set up a whole new initiative that would result not only in new manufacturers starting, but in new product lines being expanded from existing manufacturers. The request for $40,000 was made to the office, but the request was denied. The Western Diversification Office stated that it was not going to approve the $40,000 request over a two year period. Would the Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) explain why that request was rejected? It is perplexing to the 500 manufacturers which the association represents.
While he is on his feet, will he explain also why he is so afraid of members of the New Democratic Party speaking on this legislation? It is legislation that represents a very important initiative in attempts to diversify the western economy. Members of the New Democratic Party have been attempting
May 2, 1988

to participate in the debate, but time after time the Government makes an effort to curtail and restrict Members' ability to participate in a thoughtful, positive discussion on the issue.
Will the Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) explain why it is that he wants to use a form of closure on this legislation to muzzle the Opposition's voice in Parliament, which would then in a sense go against the very spirit of a parliamentary democracy?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am happy to answer my friend's question.
One of the main thrusts of the western diversification initiative is the Western Diversification Fund. The legislation presently before this House authorizes ways in which the Department can offer financial assistance for proposals and further diversification. It is that very fund which the Minister responsible for western diversification cannot approach at this time until this legislation is through the House. My hon. friend knows that. The Member gets up and pretends he does not know. The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) knows full well the thrust that has been made so far and, because the Minister responsible for the western diversification does not have access to the western diversification fund, a number of proposals have been turned down. The flexibility was not there to allow the Minister to stream them off into other existing programs. My hon. friend knows that, Madam Speaker. Western diversification has been attempting to respond to small business. Seventy per cent of the projects that have been approved to date have been awarded to small businesses and are going through existing programs. These had to be moved off to DRIE and to sub-agreements made with the provinces and so on.
The other question raised was why we on this side of this House are trying to curtail debate. We are not trying to curtail debate at all, Madam Speaker. I am the first speaker on western diversification. We will allow the Opposition all the time it requires to debate the Bill. We know that with the Opposition's actions in committee every item, every word, every clause on the western diversification Bill was filibustered by the Liberal and the NDP Members. We outlasted them in committee. When the Liberal Member left, we were able to push the Bill through to bring it back to the House. We are seeing exactly the same actions today.
The Bill is straightforward. The opposition Members cannot tell us all the amendments they want to put through. This is strictly a delay tactic and the delay is hurting western Canadians. The same New Democrats go out to western Canada and say, "Boy, are we here to help you". Here they are being run from Oshawa. They are also tools of Bob White and Shirley Carr. They will do anything and say anything if they think it will gain them one seat anywhere in Canada, and I resent that.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The time for questions and comments is now over. Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom).
Western Economic Diversification Act

Madam Speaker, I want to say a few words in this debate, if my voice holds out. First, I want to respond to my friend from Athabasca. His last comments were not very worthy of a distinguished Member like him-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: They are honest.

-when he talks about the NDP being run from Oshawa. He is using regionalism to try to divide the country. He has this fetish about Shirley Carr. I can say as a Canadian that I would rather be a friend of Shirley Carr than of Conrad Black, who is a good friend of my friend from Athabasca.
You can tell when a Member of Parliament is in trouble. The Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) is in serious trouble because he is going to be defeated by the NDP in the next campaign. I am sure you read The Globe and Mail special about this about 10 days ago, Madam Speaker. The paper wrote about the first Member of Parliament in Alberta of the Tory Party to be defeated. You can tell why the Member from Athabasca is very desperate when he speaks in the House. He is receiving a message from back home that the voters do not like the federal Conservative Party.
The Bill before the House today is a Bill ostensibly to diversify the economy in western Canada. We have been debating Bill C-113 for quite some time at second reading and at committee stage, and now we are back at third reading in the House. The whole debate about diversification in the West is a debate that has been going on for a very long time. As a western Canadian Member of Parliament since 1968 I can tell you that this has always been an issue. Those of us in western Canada feel that we have not received our fair deal from Confederation in the division of the resources of Canada and the ability of our country to have fair economic planning for all regions.
On Wednesday, Thursday, Friday and Saturday of last week I went to 12 to 14 different communities in my riding. I attended public meetings in villages and towns and meetings in farm houses in various parts of the constituency of Yorkton- Melville. There is still the feeling that the western part of Canada has not received a fair deal from Confederation. In many ways there is even more of a backlash now against the federal Government than there was a few years ago. A lot of western Canadians thought that the Conservative Party was a Party that had significant western roots and because of that many long time grievances of western Canadians would be solved, but that has not happened.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What about Virginia?

I am sure the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) from Saskatoon, when he goes there every two or three months, gets feedback that the people are not happy with the Conservative Party of Canada. People are not happy with the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney). The Minister

May 2, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
is nodding his head, I can hear him! He has also seen the poll results in his riding as I see them. The Minister of Justice is running scared not because of his qualities as a Member of Parliament. The Minister is a pretty nice, decent, likeable chap, but he is running scared because people are no longer confident in the Conservative Party of Canada and no longer confident in the leadership of the Prime Minister of this country. One reason has been the insensitivity in responding to the legitimate wishes and concerns of the people of western Canada.
What about the national energy policy that the Liberals and the NDP brought in?

When you get this kind of response from across the way you know that the problem is similar in British Columbia as well, otherwise we would not have the trumpeting of the Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. St. Germain).
Bill C-113 will not solve a lot of the problems of western Canada. The Bill will nowhere near respond to the problems that exist.
The establishment of the Western Diversification Office was first revealed to the public in August, 1987. This, you might recall, was done after the scandal at the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion where there was a cost overrun last year of $7 to $9 million. Do you remember that, Madam Speaker? There were two independent studies that confirmed a major cost overrun in DRIE because of incompetence and the misallocation of funds.
One thing the Government tried to do to respond to this cost overrun was to decentralize the whole process of regional development in Canada. It created the Atlantic Provinces Economic Opportunities Agency, an agency in northern Ontario and the Western Diversification Office in the hope of responding to the problem of regional development in Canada in order to detract from some of the negative press the Government has been receiving. I do not think there will be any real difference in the job that will be done by this agency and the job that was being done previously by various regional development or expansion offices in Canada. We have essentially the same funding, essentially the same people and essentially the same programs. Sure, the Department now has a different title, a title that is more politically attractive. Who can be against western diversification? Probably the only Hon. Member who is against it is the Hon. Member from Selkirk. It is really the same old programs, just in different clothing, for mainly electoral purposes for the Conservative Party across the way.
Over the last quarter of a century, despite all the talk, rhetoric and various programs and new initiatives in different parts of Canada, less than 3 per cent of the country's economic development dollars have been spent on regional development. That is a very, very small portion of the money that has been
allocated for economic development in Canada since 1960 or 1965. I do not think that the federal Governments over the years have been very serious about the question of regional development.
We have been told by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and by the Minister in charge of the Western Diversification Office that some $1.2 billion will be spent on regional development in western Canada, and $1.2 billion over five years works out to some $60 million per year per province. Sixty million dollars is still a fair amount of money, but $60 million per year per province is really not that much in light of what must be done. In particular, it is not that much money when we consider that some federal government programs and agreements under the previous regime will be in the process of expiring during the life of western diversification's funding over five years.
In reality, there will not be very much additional money being spent in western Canada. Sure, new money will be spent, but some of the old programs are expiring. The sunset has come for some of them. Sure, there will be new money, but looking at the balance sheet, there will not be much additional money coming to western Canada.
When the Prime Minister made the announcement back in August of last year, he said that this new money would be over and above all the existing programs. He said that this money is over and above the amounts presently flowing to western Canada under existing programs and arrangements and that these funds shall be disbursed over a five-year period in a manner that will equitably reflect the needs and the growth opportunities in our western provinces. In fact he said that on August 4, 1987.
There has been much debate over the question of the Prime Minister's claim that there will be new money with the allocation of $1.2 billion to the Western Diversification Office. Since the establishment of the Western Diversification Office involves the disbanding of the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, which was responsible for certain regional development programs, it is difficult to trace the money to ascertain what is new money and what is old money. That is a very difficult question to answer.
Sure, there will be new money coming in because there will be new programs and new budget allocations, but the original Department of DRIE is now being sacked and a lot of the programs of DRIE are being dropped or rolled into the new western diversification programs. In this new versus old money controversy, the key phrase in the Prime Minister's statement is "the amounts presently flowing under existing programs and arrangements". Again, he said that the money would be over and above the amounts presently flowing to western Canada under existing programs and arrangements.
Some of the existing programs and arrangements will be expiring, and while this money will be in addition to those arrangements and programs, if the old regime had remained in place, some of those existing programs and arrangements
May 2, 1988

would have continued. Those programs and arrangements would have spent millions and millions of dollars in all four provinces of western Canada.
How much new money is there and how much old money is there? What are the existing programs? I will give an example of what I mean, because I can see that the Minister from British Columbia is raising his eyebrows and asking questions about the new money versus old money argument. He will probably ask me about this in about 10 or 15 minutes anyway.
What are the existing programs? Three of DRIE's major program delivery tools had or are about to face major changes because of the phasing out of DRIE and the evolution of these new agencies in the different regions. The IRDP program, for example, is to expire in June of this year. That program has about 60 days to go and then the funding for that program will expire. I assume that if we did not have a Western Diversification Office or the Atlantic Opportunities Agency, a program like IRDP would be expanded beyond June of this year to finish off 1988 and to go into 1989 or 1990.
In addition to that program, many of the sub-agreements with the provinces under the ERDA programs, economic and regional development agreements, are expiring in 1989 or 1990. The costs of these programs are shared on a fifty-fifty basis between the federal Government and the provincial Government. Like IRDP, the existing ERDA arrangements will soon expire, and that old money will soon disappear. Once again, if we did not have the Western Diversification Office, I assume that new ERDA agreements would be signed between the provinces and the federal Government. I assume that millions of dollars would be spent under those programs. I simply assume that this Government would continue those programs.
Third, the Western Transportation Industrial Development Program was rejigged to become the funding program of the Western Diversification Office. Some of the ERDA programs and sub-agreements are the responsibilities of the Departments of Agriculture, Science and Technology and Transport Canada. Other sub-agreements were formerly the responsibility of DRIE and are being transferred to the Western Diversification Office. It is noted that most of these subsidiary agreements are up for renegotiation during the first five-year term of western diversification. I noted that in my remarks a few moments ago.
If we look at the moneys that are being spent and the moneys that, in all likelihood, would have been spent, we will find that there is not much if any additional money coming into western Canada. Sure, there is new money because we have program x with $100 million being scrapped to spend $100 million on program y. Program y is a brand new program with new money, but it is not additional money for my constituents and the other 6.5 million or seven million people who live in various parts of western Canada.
There are a number of other things that could be said about new money versus old money, but I do not think I have too
Western Economic Diversification Act
much time left to make my remarks. I would like to say some other things about the Bill that is before us.
As I said, I just came from a very extensive tour of my riding last week. I was in places like Dauphin, Kilaly, Sturgis, Stenan, Whitebeech, Yorkton, Melville, Preeceville, Norquay and a number of other communities. I went to about 12 or 15 communities in four days last week. My constituents kept asking time and time again why we in western Canada cannot get a fair deal from the federal Government.
I have already mentioned the problems with new money and the lack thereof coming into western Canada. We also have a problem with procurement of goods and services purchased by the federal Government. One or two cabinet Ministers are across the way, as are two Members from British Columbia, the junior Minister from Mission-Port Moody and the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Siddon). Perhaps during the question and comment period they can explain why the federal Government is spending less and less of its money proportionately in procuring items from western Canada. I have figures, which I will table, from the regional distribution of Supply and Service contracts in dollar values for western provinces as a percentage of the national government purchases in Canada for the fiscal years 1984-85, 1985-86, and 1986-87.
During the first fiscal year for which the Government had responsibility for Government of Canada spending, 1984-85, some 13.9 per cent of purchases by the Department of Supply and Services were made from western Canadian firms, businesses, and industries. In 1985-86 it went down from 13.9 per cent to 12.8 per cent. In 1986-87 it went down again to 11.5 per cent. Therefore, in the first two years of Conservative Government we had a drop in the proportion of goods and services bought in western Canada from 13.9 per cent to 11.5 per cent. That is a substantial drop of 2.4 per cent.
Why is the Government buying proportionately less and less from western Canada? In this age of high technology and computers we supply more things than we did in the past. Why is the Government, with a large western representation and many prominent westerners in the Cabinet, purchasing fewer and fewer goods and services from western Canada on a proportionate basis? Twenty-eight to 30 per cent of the population of the country is in western Canada. Why is the Government not purchasing about 25 or 30 per cent of its good and services from western Canadian enterprises and firms instead of only 11.5 per cent? That is way less than half of what our proportionate share should be.
If the federal Government had been purchasing more and more rather than less and less from the West, there would be fewer people in Alberta, Saskatchewan, British Columbia and Manitoba unemployed. I would like to know what is behind the idea of purchasing fewer and fewer items and goods in western Canada. There are two Ministers from the West in the House

May 2, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
and perhaps in the next five or ten minutes we can get an answer to that.
It is very important that this new Western Diversification Office be efficient and effective when dealing with the public of Canada. I have here a letter from a constituent of one my Saskatchewan P.C. colleagues. I do not think I should read the person's name into the record but I will read part of the letter addressed to myself. He says:
To begin with I do not think much of the Western Diversification Program.
I will explain the enclosed material which are copies. When I first heard of this program I felt that finally a government program is available to help a small western business. I was not looking for a handout, only backing to help get a loan. At the end of Aug. 1987, 1 wrote western diversification explaining my situation. Towards the end of Sept. 1987, I received a letter from western diversification and an assigned project number 4000.8-G5.
Feb. 15, 1988 having not heard from these people I wrote a letter asking for a status report. I again wrote the same letter on Mar. 1, 1988. On Mar. 7, 1988 I received a call from a lady in this office telling me my application had been rejected.
I told her I expected as much as I had noted in the paper only large enterprises seemed to qualify. She said that was not true as there were a number of small businesses that would be named shortly. To date I have seen nothing. I asked to have a letter of rejection sent.
After two weeks and still no letter I phoned again.
You are cutting me off, Madam Speaker. I realize that my time is up. This is someone from Saskatchewan who applied for backing for a loan for a small business. He received no response whatsoever month after month. When he did get a response it was a telephone call, after prodding, saying that his project had been rejected.
I do hope that when this program is established in western Canada it will be efficiently and well run so that the positive aspects of the program are available to all western Canadians equally regardless of where they may live.

Madam Speaker, I would like to make a comment or two and then ask the Hon. Member for York-ton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) a question. As chairman of the committee I thought it was very unfortunate that the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville was unable to attend all the meetings. He was busy elsewhere. He certainly made a very valuable contribution to the meeting which he did attend. I want to thank him for his good sense and logic. In my view the debate in the committee was very sound.
I think the language of the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) was rather badly chosen when he said that certain witnesses "were not permitted to come". None of the witnesses which he mentioned asked to come. It was not a case of not being permitted, they never asked either myself or the clerk to appear.
The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville dealt with DRIE and the Western Economic Diversification Program. He wondered whether there would be any difference. I suggest that there will be a vast difference. For instance, only one area in the entire Province of Alberta qualified under the DRIE program. Consequently, the program was of little use to the
Province of Alberta. The Whitecourt area was the only area in the entire Province of Alberta which qualified under DRIE.
I think that western diversification will be a different program. There are two major differences between DRIE and western diversification. Under western diversification the board may make loans and it may guarantee loans. That will make a world of difference as far as the Province of Alberta is concerned.
We are talking about diversification with regard to agriculture and oil and gas. One of the best examples is the shortfall of the Crow. If the shortfall of the Crow were paid to the producers in the Province of Alberta there would be diversification galore without any extra funds, yet we are giving very little consideration to the shortfall of the Crow.
The other example I have is also based on agriculture, that is, making fuel from ethane and methynol. We could use millions of bushels of wheat which would create a tremendous new industry and provide diversification. However, there must be money provided for that.
In the view of the Hon. Member would these two items not help a great deal to make the Western Economic Diversification Program more successful than the DRIE program has been so far?

Madam Speaker, I want to thank the Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) for his question and his comments. He pointed out my absence at the committee. I was there for one meeting. I was not there for the others because, as he probably knows, I was travelling with the Energy Committee with the Member for Calgary South (Mrs. Sparrow). We were studying the question of nuclear waste. The Member has been around politics for a long time and knows that you cannot split yourself into two or three. I am very sorry that I was not able to attend all the committee meetings but I certainly followed them very closely.
I agree with the Member for Bow River that there are some positive things in this program. I said that in the main it is basically the old program, as far as I am concerned. However, he did mention a couple of things which make it a bit more attractive to people across western Canada.
One of my concerns, which is perhaps a concern of the Hon. Member too, is that we do not want the program to be aimed in a major sense at big business. I am primarily interested in small business. I have here an editorial from the Saskatoon Star Phoenix, which is one of the big dailies in the Province of Saskatchewan. They are concerned about the fact that so far the money has been going out to big business.
The other concern which I have, which I did not have a chance to mention before, is that some of the money spent so far has not been spent on diversification. It has been spent for economic expansion. Of course, I am not opposed to economic expansion. I want to expand agriculture, the potash industry and so on for western Canada. However, as I asked the
May 2, 1988

Minister in the committee, if this is the Western Diversification Office, why is not more money being targeted for genuine diversification in western Canada?
I refer again to the editorial in the Star-Phoenix which states that: "However, with the first two high-profile announcements about specific funding under our diversification initiative involving $75 million in soil erosion and $5 million in potash marketing, taxpayers may well be wondering what diversification really does mean to the Government of Canada. The spending on these two programs is welcome". The editorial goes on to say: "Anything that enhances the farming sector and potash mining is good news for Saskatchewan people. But this is not moving the province or the West in general away from dependence on the familiar staple industries. So far, from what has been made public about projects approved under the initiative, it is just another economic aid package: welcome, certainly, but not the stuff of new directions in an unusually moribund western economy".
I suggest to my hon. friend from Alberta, as does this article, that we welcome economic expansion and economic development. However, this program is supposed to be one to diversify.
I wonder, as I am sure he wonders as a western Member of Parliament, how much of this money will be spent on items to diversify the economy of western Canada.
We are all interested in diversifying. We love agriculture, mining, potash, oil and gas and forestry in British Columbia, and want to do what we can in those areas, but we do not want to be held solely dependent on those resources.
It appears, not only to us but to independent observers, that so far the major part of this program is directed toward economic expansion rather than economic diversification. If so, it should be called the western diversification and expansion office. However, if it is meant for diversification, let it proceed in that way.

Madam Speaker, I want to make a few comments in response to some of the points made by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) and to answer a particular question he put to us.
First, I am pleased to learn that the Hon. Member supports the establishment of this western diversification program. I only urge that he and his Party get on with allowing us to provide the program with the full legal weight and effect that is required in order to deliver these important initiatives in western Canada.
The Hon. Member made an issue of the percentages with respect to procurement by the various Departments of Government through the Department of Supply and Services. I will grant that in regard to specific percentages there is a trend with which we are not particularly pleased. However, to be fair, I think the Hon. Member should give the numbers in
Western Economic Diversification Act
terms of dollars expended by each government Department through the Department of Supply and Services for the procurement of government supply. He may well see quite a different trend.
In fact, I think it is unfair only to deal with the statistics on a percentage basis with respect to procurement of the normal supply to Government of such things as pencils, paper clips and the routine supply that all Governments procure from time to time. He should not do so without considering the larger picture and comparing it with those percentage figures, not just the dollar amounts which have increased substantially in western Canada since this Government took office, but the unprecedented level of Federal Government support for industrial diversification in British Columbia and western Canada.
My own riding is a typical example of that expansion. There has been some $ 100 million worth of assistance to enterprise in the nature of industrial diversification in such sophisticated areas as the advanced aerospace industry. We opened a new automated precision machining plant in Delta, British Columbia a few days ago. That is a multimillion dollar investment. There are many examples, through various companies that are on the leading edge of technology and applied technology, of unprecedented things occurring in western Canada. I have calculated a total of more than $2 billion worth of initiatives by this Government in the Province of British Columbia alone. That is far in excess of anything previously committed by way of government initiatives in British Columbia.
For example, there is the $268 million North warning contract to Microtek The western diversification initiative itself will bring tens of millions of dollars to British Columbia, and is already beginning to do so.
